subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak today in the debate on the Main Estimates for the year 1986-87. Hon. Members will recall that on February 27, 1986, I tabled the Main Estimates for the current year which amount to $107 billion. On that occasion, I advised the House that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) had announced the
June 10, 1986

day before, in his Budget, that there would be an additional expenditure cutback of $500 million which was not included in the Estimates. For several months Treasury Board has been working diligently with the various departments in order to identify the parameters of this cutback. Although a number of areas have yet to be examined and a number of details must still be worked out, much of the work has been completed, and I can assure Hon. Members that details of this cutback will be available very shorty.
With the $500 million expenditure cutback, the growth rate of our projected expenditures decreases to 3.9 per cent, the lowest rate recorded in 24 years.
Roughly two thirds of the total Main Estimates represents statutory spending, in other words, expenditures made in accordance with existing legislation. The remaining third, $37.5 billion, represents expenditures which Parliament is being asked to vote or authorize. The clearest indication, in the short term, of the Government's firm resolve to reduce spending is the control it exercises over non-statutory expenditures. That is why I was pleased to announce, when tabling the Main Estimates last February, that the rate of growth of these expenditures was virtually zero. Mr. Speaker, if we exclude increases arising from our commitments in the areas of national defence and external aid, our operational costs will decline by 4.2 per cent.
Until quite recently, statutory and non-statutory spending in particular had been increasing quite rapidly. From 1974-75 to 1984-85, the Government's total expenditures increased by an average of 13.4 per cent annually, well above the average inflation rate of 8.8 per cent. As a proportion of the gross national product, federal expenditures have increased from about 15 per cent in 1965 to over 20 per cent in 1975 and to nearly 26 per cent in 1984. In 1984-85, servicing the national debt absorbed 32 per cent of federal revenues and represented 21 per cent of total public spending. This was the situation confronting the Government the day after the election: a deteriorating financial situation despite an apparently improving economy.

To achieve sustainable growth and regain control over expenditures, the Government developed a plan to reduce the real level of Government spending and reverse the upward trend in the federal debt to GNP ratio. It had to establish a sound fiscal policy that would support, rather than hamper, economic renewal and redefine the role of Government in a way that would help improve management and eliminate inefficiencies and obsolete programs.
The Government did not waste time. Within a few months of taking office, I announced a number of measures to reduce by $4.2 billion the federal Government's budgetary and nonbudgetary requirements for the 1985-86 fiscal year. In deciding where to reduce expenditures, the Government followed a principle of equity which would guard against shifting the burden to the poor or the under-privileged in our
Supply
society and which would balance the impact among the various regions of the country and sectors of the economy. This was an important first step by a new Government to streamline operations and reduce expenditures. Virtually every Department was affected by the expenditure and program review.
Controlling expenditures is not an easy task but it is one to which this Government was and continues to be firmly committed. The results are in. The Government has clearly regained firm control over federal expenditures. Although the detailed accounts have not been finalized, all indications are that actual program expenditures for 1985-86, that is, total Government spending excluding public debt charges, went down. This is the first decline in Government program expenditures in the post-war period.
In order to achieve its goals, the Government could not be satisfied with merely applying general measures of restraint to its programs. It had to examine the very raison d'etre of many of these programs and eliminate waste and duplication. The Government, therefore, set up a ministerial task force on program review under the chairmanship of my colleague, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen), to examine specific programs, identify areas of overlap and opportunities for improving the efficiency and effectiveness of Government programs. Private sector volunteers worked closely with public servants in 19 study teams to examine virtually all government programs.
We have already benefited greatly from the work of the ministerial task force on program review. As Members know, this resulted in a number of recommendations which continue to form the basis for program reductions. Some duplication has already been eliminated, some operations have already been streamlined, and meaningful savings have already been achieved.
The Government is committed also to further improving the management of its operations. A number of changes have been implemented recently to improve the management of the Government's assets. I would like to touch briefly on some of the most important ones.
First, a ministerial task force on privatization has been created, chaired by myself, as President of the Treasury Board, to review systematically the potential for privatization of Crown corporations or changes to their status to more suitably reflect public policy objectives. Unless there is a compelling public policy purpose to retain a given Crown corporation, it will be put on the market or it will be wound up.

A number of corporations such as Loto Canada, Canagrex and the Canada Museums Construction Corporation are being phased out or have already disappeared. The Northern Transportation Company Limited was sold last July for $27 million, followed in August by the sale of the Canada Development Corporation, resulting in revenues amounting to $132 million, with another $132 million to follow within twelve months.

June 10, 1986
Supply
More recently, de Havilland Limited was sold to Boeing for $155 million and Canadian Arsenals was sold to the SNC Group for $92.2 million. Thanks to this policy, we have handed over to the private sector activities for which it is better suited.
As I have already indicated on several occasions, Mr. Speaker, privatization will be done with discernment and care. There will be no fire sales. The Government intends to get a fair return for what it sells. It is also quite aware of the needs of the management and staff of those corporations. When Canadian Arsenals was sold, for instance, we signed a reciprocity agreement with the buyer to make sure that the employees' pension rights would be protected.
As well, the Government takes into consideration the impact of these sales on consumers and provincial Governments. This is why the Northern Transportation Company was sold to a buyer who is committed to maintain services in northern communities.
Second, innovative measures have been taken to improve the management of federal real estate, including:
1.	An over-all action plan aimed at disposing of surplus or little-used real estate; real estate up for sale in 1985-86 was valued at about $200 million, and revenues from this source in 1986-87 will amount to $247 million;
2.	The decision-making process was separated from the operational process, with resulting changes in the mandates of the Treasury Board and Public Works Canada;
3.	A new real estate management office was established and responsibilities related to real estate were redefined.
Third, the Government has also taken a more productive approach concerning the management of public funds, which made it possible to save money thanks to this new approach:
First, the Government pays its suppliers at the right moment, neither too early so as no to lose accruing interests nor too late so it would have to pay interests. In addition, we resort to travelers' cheques, credit cards and payments by electronic facilities whenever it is to our advantage;
Second, the Government has been attempting to reduce amounts owed to the Crown, thanks to more effective recovery methods;
Finally, the Government uses various mechanisms for deposits, transfers-including electronic transfers-and bank accounts consolidation.
We have imposed severe restraints with respect to person-years, the unit used to measure and control the size of the public service. The Government believes that its essential services can be maintained at reduced costs, thanks in part to downsizing the public service.
We have already begun to implement a five-year program to reduce the size of the Public Service. The Estimates I tabled
on February 27 show a reduction of some 5,500 person years, or 2.1 per cent from the previous year. This alone will save $150 million in 1986-87. Over the next four years a further 1 per cent reduction per year will be implemented so that by 1990-1991 the person year reduction will total 15,000. The accumulated savings to the taxpayers will be $1.5 billion with recurring annual savings of approximately $500 million.
The reduction in the size of the Public Service is being achieved in a humane and orderly manner, thanks to the improved Work Force Adjustment Policy which this Government implemented a year ago. The policy states that employees whose jobs are no longer required will, as far as possible, be redeployed within the Public Service with retraining, if necessary. Briefly, major improvements made last year to the policy include, first, that the minimum notice to an employee whose job is being abolished was increased from three months to four months, although departments endeavour to give at least six months' notice. Laid-off persons are now eligible for retraining and those accepting lower level positions are provided with up to one year's salary protection. The Work Force Adjustment Policy is among the best, if not the best, being offered by major employers in Canada today.
In order to build upon this policy, I announced at the beginning of last February a staffing freeze in the Public Service. In a sense, the freeze can be viewed as a bit of shock therapy. I wanted departments to sit up and take notice of the situation. I wanted them to fully understand the fundamental change which was taking place. I wanted their full cooperation in applying the Work Force Adjustment Policy. At the end of May, after reviewing the situation, I became convinced that the continuing efforts being made to place affected employees were not in jeopardy. As a result, I lifted the freeze.
Our rate of success in managing the reduction in the size of the Public Service has been very encouraging. Of the 5,200 employees affected this year, about 3,500 have been, or will be, offered another job either in their own department, in another department or in the private sector. I am confident that the actual number of lay-offs in this reduction exercise will be no higher than 500 by the end of 1986-87. Should circumstances change, I will take the necessary steps to ensure that the number of lay-offs does not exceed these projections.
Improving the Work Force Adjustment Policy is but one of the many improvements we have brought to the management of human resources in the Public Service. Other improvements include: first, a comprehensive framework has been introduced for human resource planning which integrates management of this vital resource with the planning and management of programs and expenditures. Second, Treasury Board has negotiated a master agreement with the Professional Institute of the Public Service. As far as the negotiation of a master agreement with the Public Service Alliance of Canada is concerned, a binding conciliation board has been established and I expect proceedings will begin this month. Third, a voluntary early retirement program was implemented for
June 10, 1986

senior officials. This initiative enabled 535 senior public servants to retire. The program was designed not only to help resolve a serious problem resulting from reduced turnover among the higher ranks by opening up new career opportunities for talented public service managers, but to produce payroll savings, since about half of the vacated positions are being eliminated. Fourth, a new productivity bonus system will be introduced to further encourage efficient and cost-effective management in the federal public sector. The bonus will apply for the 1986-87 fiscal year. It will be based on performance, more specifically on savings achieved while respecting objectives related to such things as affirmative action, safety, security and so forth. Fifth, various new initiatives have been implemented to promote employment equity in the Public Service and in Crown corporations for women, aboriginal peoples, disabled persons, visible minorities, to improve access to federal facilities for the disabled and generally to improve the working conditions for public sector employees.

Other improvements have been made concerning management, and these have contributed to lower costs, increased revenues, and a more manageable Government apparatus. I will mention only three, Mr. Speaker.
First, the general costs of departments and organizations have been reduced and a stricter control has been imposed on future growth in this sector so as to boost productivity and improve management even more.
Second, strict new measures for examining potential loan guarantees have been implemented so as to minimize the risk of Government losses as a result of payment defaults and to share risks more equitably with private sector interests.
Third, the Government is actively considering cost recovery options to reduce the spending tendency and to distribute more equitably among the direct beneficiaries and taxpayers in general the burden of providing public goods and services.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the 1986-87 Main Estimates being considered today are the result of eighteen months of serious Financial planing. An efficient administration, rationalized operations and substantial savings, such are the results obtained to date, all of which reflects a radical change compared with the previous decade. As our resources are scarce, we have to use them wisely. We have to try to spend less and better.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) and to tell him immediately that we are all for an efficient and effective Public Service. We are also all in favour of a more efficient program to get better value for our tax dollars.
The Minister has announced a new policy of his Government to grant a productivity premium to non-unionized management
Supply
workers. He will recall that I have already asked him in this House what criteria would apply to the administration of this program and why it is that managers can get a productivity premium when, in fact, the public servants themselves are the ones who produce. I asked the Minister a while ago to tell us what the criteria would be, but he has not done so. I wonder whether, today, since this is the last day of supply, he could tell the House what criteria will be used under the management premium program.	>
Could he give us a few examples and also maybe tell us why this money, which will be used as a sort of management incentive to improve to the effectiveness of Government programs, was not redistributed in the pay cheques, for instance, to encourage all employees to be more productive? Why create a climate which is not quite healthy by providing a productivity premium to Public Service managers since, at least according to my own research, no other Government, except perhaps in some American state, has a productivity premium? Would he give us further details on the criteria and applicability of the program and would he also tell us why he decided on a management premium instead of redistributing all this money as employee incentives?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext:
When the Budget was brought down, a productivity bonus for managers was announced that would promote and reward efficiency and increase productivity within the Public Service.
I am now being asked about criteria. The criteria for this bonus, further details are to be released very shorthly-consist essentially in rewarding performance beyond that normally expected of managers in the Public Service. The point has just been raised that this is an unhealthy practice, but I would simply like to point out to the Hon. Member for Ottawa- Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) that it is a practice that may be found in almost all large companies in the private sector, a practice which I think has produced good results. And in line with the present Government's managerial approach which is aimed at introducing management forms similar to those in the private sector-I already mentioned cash management which has meant savings of hundreds of millions of dollars by introducing systems copied from the private sector ... In the same vein, I am confident that the incentive for efficiency provided by this bonus will produce the expected results.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party

I have a short supplementary, Mr. Speaker. The Minister said: We will have the criteria in a few days, this Department's Main Estimates are now before the House, and the debate is supposed to end today. Why doesn't the Minister promise the House that today, this afternoon or at some time between now and 10 o'clock this evening, he will come to the House and explain what these criteria are? How does he expect us to adopt a new program sight unseen, as it were? I must admit, I don't know whether the Minister understands my question, but since it is a completely new program in the public sector ... In the private sector, it works because of the profit incentive-the more you sell the more you get-but in

the public sector, service is what counts. So I my question to the Minister is: Why doesn't he come to the House and tell us before the end of the day's, proceedings how this is going to work?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out to the Hon. Member that the specific details of the program have not been determined, so I cannot give them. They still have to be worked out, but a lot has been done already. This is a new program that we intend to table in the House as soon as it is ready to be tabled.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in a sense my question to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) is supplementary to those asked by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier). I am concerned about the trend we see coming from the Minister. In the private sector it is fairly easy to measure performance in order to reward it. It is based on whether one's department is more productive than others in terms of profits, or whether it is generating more revenue, sales or whatever. What I am hearing more and more, and this is what concerns me, is that the Government seems to be running Canada as if it were General Motors or the Royal Bank of Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext: It's not that good.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext: Does he see running a Government as being quite different from running a private corporation? What are the distinguishing differences?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there are a number of very important distinguishing factors. Obviously, we in the public sector have great concern for the safety and security of the public in terms of services. We run a number of programs which are socially oriented. From this point of view I will be the first to admit that Government is very different from the private sector. However, in terms of management practices, while we do not have many profit centres, we do have a great number of cost centres.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext: Should we?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext: The cost centres can be managed by using sound management principles that have been proven to be successful in the private sector. When the Hon. Member says that we seem to want to run the Government of Canada, from a management point of view and not a policy point of view, like one would run GM or another large corporation, I say yes, that is true. To date the results have been very encouraging. For the first time in the post-war period we are seeing a decline in the most critical portion of our Government expenditures.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext: Which is?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987

speechtext: Is that how you measure success? It's easy to be successful, just lay off half the public servants.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have four questions which I would like to ask the Minister in order to have his comments. The first relates to the Minister's comment that the Public Service will be reduced in numbers. Recently we have received reports that in fact the numbers in the Public Service have gone up rather than down. I would ask the Minister to put an explanation on the record for that.
Second, there are reports that in efforts to reduce the Public Service the four target groups in employment equity are being impacted unfairly, particulary women, disabled, native people and the visible minorities, because their seniority is much less than that of the traditional groups in the Public Service.
Third, I would like the Minister to comment on whether or not the visible minorities were a target group within the Public Service for employment equity prior to September of 1984 when the present Government was elected.
Fourth, I would like the Minister to comment on the electronic transfer of funds, bearing in mind that prior to the election of 1984 our Party, which now forms the Government, took the position that there should be, and there were great savings to be had in the electronic transfer of funds. I believe something in the order of $250 million in savings was estimated at that time. Apparently, there has been no action taken since that time. One of the impressions that I have been given for that is that while there would be a saving to the Government there would be a loss of revenue to the Post Office. That loss of revenue would increase the deficit of the Post Office and there is great resistence from the Post Office on that point.
Will the Minister comment on my four questions, please?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext:
The first question raised, Mr. Speaker, was with respect to the apparent contradiction in terms of the numbers of public servants. The numbers that were published recently were year-end numbers for the last fiscal year. The reduction program begins in 1986-87. That is one explanation. In other words, because it is dealing with a period in which there was no reduction in person-years it is quite normal to have seen a slight increase.
The other point I would like to make is that some of the numbers that I saw were not consistent with the same data base that we are using. There were data base differences which perhaps can explain some of the increases that were there. The major reason is that we are dealing with last year while the program essentially deals with the forthcoming year.
In terms of employment equity, throughout the process we have first indicated very clearly that Departments should

When the Minister says that the fiscal position of the Government has improved substantially, as he likes to claim, or has improved marginally during his tenure as President of the Treasury Board, what does he really mean? Has he magically reduced expenditures in some intelligent way? Has he been fiscally responsible? Let us ask ourselves what he really means.
We know that under one program alone, the Established Programs Financing, the Government is cutting back $8 billion from funds that ordinarily would be transferred to the provinces. Has the Government cut out $8 billion worth of waste? Has it identified $8 billion worth of expenditures that need not continue in order to provide Canadians with the level of service to which they have become accustomed? Has the Government found, lying around hidden in the tunnels and corridors of official Ottawa power, $8 billion worth of wasteful employees, expenditures and programs? No, Mr. Speaker.
The Minister is pounding himself on the chest for having transferred $8 billion of debt to the provinces. He took $8 billion of the federal deficit out of his pocket and passed it over to the provincial Governments. Then he rose in the House, pounded his chest and said: "Look how much better the bottom line is". What is the Government's attitude about that? The Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall), appearing before the finance committee, said that provinces are stuck with federal funding cuts.
I expected the Minister to rise today to give us a list of all those insidious, terrible, negative, wasteful programs that he had found during his search for fiscal responsibility and to lay them before the House of Commons and say: "Look what I found, look at these nasty, wasteful programs". However, there was not one single example given by the Minister of such a program. Why? Because he has not identified waste. He has not done his job. He has not avoided duplication. He has transferred a debt for what all Canadians regard as very essential services, health and education, out of federal jurisdiction and onto the backs of provincial Governments.
What does the Minister of State for Finance say about that? She said that we are stuck with those transfers and went on to say that the provinces should not complain too much because the provinces now enjoy the benefits of Canada's strong economic performance. They understand that the decision made by the Government to load onto the backs of the provinces $8 billion in additional expenditures ordinarily paid by the Government of Canada for health and education will have two results. There will be 10 different levels of Canadian citizenship across the country, all in the name of an exercise designed to allow the Minister to rise, pound his chest and say that the bottom line is better. It brought in the largest tax increase, both through sales taxes and personal incomes taxes, that Canada has seen in decades. Not only did the Government bring in the largest tax increase but it applied it unevenly as well. Those at the lower end of the income scale making $15,000 per year will pay about 35 per cent or 36 per cent more in aggregate taxes over the next four or five years and those at the higher end of the income tax scale who are making a couple of hundred thousand dollars per year are going to pay 2 per cent more in aggregate taxes over the next four or five years. That is another way the Minister has gotten rid of waste. That is more so-called waste which he has cut out, not on the backs of the provinces, but on the backs of Canada's poor citizens. It gets progressively worse as one goes from the top of the income scale to the bottom of it. Therefore, those who can afford it the least are paying the most.

Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) who referred to the new version of "The Life of Brian". I think it ought to be called "The Fool on the Hill". today with this transfer of debt off the back of the federal Government and on to the backs of provincial Governments and ordinary Canadians.
During the course of his remarks, the Minister mentioned the ministerial task force on privatization. It is evident to all Canadians-and nowhere is it more evident than it is to those Canadians who live in the rural parts of the country-that the Government has moved to a strict user-pay policy. The Government of Canada is saying to Canadians that no matter where they live, no matter what conditions under which they live, the only facilities or services they shall be offered by the Government are those for which they can pay. Also it is saying that if and when they cannot pay 100 per cent of the cost of those services and facilities, they shall not have them. That is what the Government is saying.
In Clause 4 of Bill C-75 respecting the Canada Shipping Act, the Government is saying to people who live in Canada's north that future ice-breaking and coast guard services which it provides shall be paid for by them. If you cannot afford those services, you shall not have them and if without them you cannot live comfortably in Canada's north, that is your problem.
The Government is saying to the fishermen of Atlantic Canada in Bill C-75, Clause 4, that you shall pay 100 per cent of the cost of the Coast Guard if you are in trouble at sea. If you think you cannot afford to pay the cost of the Coast Guard services, you better not call and take your chances on your own, because we will bill you if we come to rescue you. That is the kind of mentality the Government has adopted. It is a user-pay concept.
What is the result, Mr. Speaker? We have the Government of Canada contemplating a $500 million expenditure for a Canadian Coast Guard vessel to protect our sovereignty in the north because the Americans can plough the northern waters with the Polar Sea whenever they feel like it, that is, ever since this administration has been in office. This administration always gives the Americans the benefit of the doubt. The Government should be investing in the north and putting money into the Mackenzie to dredge and widen it so people who live in the north can better utilize their major means of transportation. Rather than getting rid of the extra fees and penalizing people who live in the north, the Government should be putting some money into providing services. The best claim to Canadian sovereignty we can have is by having Canadians live in the north, not by having a $500 million icebreaker.
The user-pay concept, which the Government is bringing forward that says only those who live in large population centres who have enough numbers, enough of a market mentality to justify government services, is putting constraints on many Canadians' sense of citizenship. It is saying to Canadians in Atlantic Canada that you are damned if you do not live in Toronto. It is saying to people who live in Alberta
where the economy has seen a downturn you are damned as well if you do not live in Toronto.

She was there and knows the cost of renting chalets and limousines. She knows what it costs to take batteries of supporters with her. She thought she would benefit other Canadians by writing "Europe on $5,000 a Day".
This falls right on the heels of the pronouncement yesterday of the new Canadian film corporation, "Prime Minister Productions". Now we find out that wherever the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) goes he has a film crew with him to film every gesture so that the "Life of Brian" will unfold for Canadians in the years ahead. Much to the chagrin, I would say, of the Monty Python group who are very concerned about this new development and the threat to their fine film.
This is not the beginning, this is the end of a long sequence of unbelievable abuses of public funds. During the election campaign the Prime Minister, time after time, railed at Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau and his huge staff in the Prime Minister's Office. Those people were being used for political purposes. It was a dastardly deed and an abuse of public spending. There were 60 people, after all, in the Prime Minister's Office. He would go back and explain that Mr. Pearson as Prime Minister had just a handful of people, but here is Prime Minister Trudeau who has expanded his office to include 60 people and all kinds of equipment and offices. The Prime Minister said that must be stopped. A lot of us thought that meant we must cut back on the number. As soon as he got into office he said he was going to change it. He was going to double the staff. He would have 120 people on his payroll as personal political advisers and hacks. That is not what we expected.

speechtext:
I think the important point is this. No Government in the world has ever bailed out uninsured bank depositors to this extent, except the Conservative Government of Canada. It is funny how you can find $1 billion over a weekend when we have women's resource centres closing their doors and transitional homes can no longer function because they are not getting their budget of $35,000 a year to operate. Those are the kind of priorities we are dealing with. When the Government says it is going to put the lid on certain kinds of spending, that means certain selected areas of spending, and others, will be expanded.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) has been very straightforward with us today. I do not criticize him in my comments today. I want to make that perfectly clear. I believe he is honourably motivated and attempting to do the best job he can. However, I am going to criticize his Government and some of the decision-making going on outside of his office.
Just the other day we heard about the consultants being hired by all the committees. These consultants are getting contracts for a few months and they are not being paid $200 a
14156

June 10, 1986
Supply
day or $300 a day or $500 a day, or even $800 a day like Macdonald. Some are being paid up to $1,000 a day, day after day after day. We are seeing more and more of that kind of spending. We may be laying off public servants, but when we look at the amount of money spent on contracts for friends and colleagues then we get a clear picture of how serious the Government is about cutting back.
We now have an opportunity to reflect for a moment or two on some of the myths which I think the Government has perpetuated over the last few months. The Government feels that government is like a business and should be run like a corporation, a shoe store chain or McDonald's. The President of the Treasury Board indicated he feels we should reward managers for productivity. The question is, how do you measure productivity in Government? I do not want to suggest for a moment that that is impossible, but the Minister says they do it in the private sector. Of course they do. It is very clear how you measure effectiveness and efficiency in the private sector; it is what the quarterly balance sheet tells you. However, it is a little different in Government.
There are other needs which Government must serve. The Government is charged with the responsibility of maintaining peace and security, and ensuring the respective rights and liberties of its citizens. It has to ensure greater justice among its citizens and act as a collective agent for the people in ensuring that the means of production serve the needs of the people. The purpose of Government is to be people-oriented in a sensible, wise and fiscally responsible way. I believe we have gotten out of control. When you run Canada like Ronald McDonald runs the McDonald's chain, then we have some real difficulties.
Another myth that the Government needs to be caught up on is the recognition of a deficit problem. The Government says we have a deficit problem, and we do. Then it goes on to say that Government spending is out of control. Probably in some areas Government spending is out of control. However, what the Government does not point to is the hidden spending which is beginning to accelerate. There are hundreds of millions, indeed billions of dollars in hidden spending called taxes we do not collect anymore. We have tax give-aways, loopholes, deferrals and incentives to the private corporate sector. They amount to billions and billions and billions of dollars each year that the Government fails to collect. That is one of the major causes of our deficit.
The Economic Council of Canada recently said that the principal cause of the federal Government's past and present fiscal plight has been the shortfall of revenue. During the past decade over-all expenditure growth had been relatively restrained. Look at some of the tax expenditures which have grown exponentially over the last 10 years. For example, the capital cost allowance and fast depreciation is now costing us $2,215 billion a year. I think it is fair to ask, are we getting good value for that expenditure? That is an incredible amount of money.
Then we go on to the special resource measures to encourage companies to explore for gas and oil. That is costing us $1,210 billion annually. The capital gains exemption costs $3.6 billion last year. On top of that, now that the Government has decided not to tax capital gains for individuals up to $500,000, there is an additional $1.2 billion cost to the taxpayer.
We have to think about this. When you look at all those write-offs and deductions and loopholes, what is the result? We are spending billions and billions and billions of dollars. May I humbly suggest that if the Government is serious about reducing the deficit, rather than hacking away at the single parents' family allowance payments each month, rather than hacking away at the Department of the Environment and laying off hundreds of people, rather than hacking away at the small grants to women's resource centres or transition houses or homes for battered women, support for Elizabeth Fry organizations and so on, rather than hack away at all of those programs, why not close off some of the major tax programs that provide us with perhaps limited return for unbelievable amounts of money.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), in a speech to the Canadian Tax Foundation on November 28, 1984, said:
Our recent figures indicate that the effect of tax incentives has been to reduce the average federal corporate income tax rate from 36 per cent to 15 per cent. When the benefits from special tax incentives are added together we are looking, in some instances, at an extraordinarily generous level of assistance.
Those are the words of the Minister of Finance referring to our corporate tax system, "extraordinarily generous". I wonder when we are asking Canadians generally to tighten their belts, to cut back wherever possible, to reduce their expenditures, if it is not reasonable to also ask the corporate sector which is receiving, by the Minister of Finance's own words, "extraordinarily generous levels of assistance" to also cut back.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Frazee of the Royal Bank of Canada recently stood up and said he was prepared to cut back on all of these excessive corporate generous tax programs and financial relief programs. I suspect that that is an area where the Government should be looking.
As my friend indicated earlier, increases in the sales tax and excise tax now are costing Canadian families dearly. I think if you were to take the time and add up all of the cost to the average Canadian family as a result of this new Government's budgets and economic statement-if you added up the sales tax, the excise tax, the increase in personal tax rates-it would come to $1,305 in additional costs per year per Canadian family. That is an awful lot of money that is coming now out of the families and the communities of Canada to enable the Government to continue with these "extraordinarily general levels of assistance" primarily to the corporate sector.
The best information we have now regarding the corporate tax rate dates back to 1983. That is the most up-to-date statistic that we have of a general nature. If you were to look at those figures you would notice that tens of thousands of
June 10, 1986

profitable businesses in Canada in 1983 did not pay a single penny in income tax. In many cases there are good and legitimate reasons for that. I would suggest that some of those tens of thousands of profitable businesses that paid no tax should be paying their fair share in order to relieve us of the deficit problem that faces our country.
Let me go on to refer to a few other items. I notice again that our Minister of Finance in a speech to the Canadian Economics Association in Montreal on May 30, 1985 had this famous quote: "No matter how we define the term Canada has an acute shortage of rich people". He indicated presumably by that that he wants to make more and more people richer. When you consider the tax changes that lead in that direction, when you consider the increase in sales tax, which is a very regressive tax, an increase in the excise tax, which again is a regressive tax, when you consider items such as the tax free capital gains provision, or the tax system, it looks as though the Minister is really trying to provide more opportunities for the wealthy of Canada. Unfortunately it is on the backs of ordinary working Canadians. This is the trend.
When the Government provides us now with its estimates of $116,740 million and asks us now to pass this because we ought to feel good about where the country is going and how the country is being managed, I have to look for some evidence of that. I have to look for evidence that things have improved significantly. I would not say that there have not been improvements. I would not say that there have not been improved processes. I would not say that the Government has turned a totally blind eye in reforming the tax system and other areas. When we ask ourselves as parliamentarians where Canada is going in the various sectors, where we going in terms of Canada's fishing industry, I wonder if the Members of the House could stand up and say, "Well, folks, here is where Canada is going in the next five or ten years with our fishing industry".
Let us take our textile industry. What is the future of the textile industry in Canada? Where are we going? Again, after two years in office I do not think that that is an unreasonable question for a Member of Parliament to be asking for some very clear direction.
Really what I see, as an Opposition parliamentarian, is the Liberal approach to governing Canada, modified in some ways, with more advantages going to some of the wealthier Canadians and more advantages going to the large corporate sector. By and large we have the same kind of direction, which in my mind is no direction that I can see. I do not see any clear pathway or clear strategy or clear blueprint or clear plan for the future. All I see is the Government muddling through, week by week, trying to work its way through and keep out of trouble, primarily, in the various sectors.
In closing, I simply want to say that a Government that makes as a priority the public relations and image, and so on, of our Prime Minister, and feels quite comfortable in spending money on creating the "Life of Brian" film: when we have Ministers of the Crown touring Europe and writing books on

"Europe on $5,000 a Day", that is the kind of activity that really betrays the changes that have come as a result of a change in Government-very, very little, indeed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have some very strong feelings about the point raised by the Hon. Member. My views are a result of my experience as a Member of Parliament from British Columbia who has just seen the provincial Government actually decimate that province. Not only have the social programs been cut to the bone, half of the bones are missing. The British Columbia economy is on its knees because the R. B. Bennett approach to resolving the economic and social challenges facing that province was used to the extreme, with disastrous results. That provincial Government expected just that kind of activity from its senior public servants. They were expected to make serious cut-backs in the public service, and I suggest that the record is clear for anyone who wants to see how the Socreds have mismanaged the situation in that province so badly. Their approach is the last model that anyone would want to use, and that is why some of us are so concerned that we see a similar model being applied here, but not to the same extreme. Fortunately, only the Social Credit Government in British Columbia is that silly.
There is a certain similarity with the approach taken by the President of the Treasury Board. He agreed that one way to measure effectiveness is if one can reduce the public sector. The easiest way to reduce the discretionary spending is presumably by laying off public servants. If that is the measurement for effectiveness or efficiency, one simply has to lay off half of one's Department or cut half the services provided by the Department and one will receive rewards or bonuses of one kind or another. It is that type of mindless incentive program about which we are concerned.
I am not suggesting that it is not possible to implement an evaluation system whereby outstanding performance by a public servant can be rewarded, but we want to know the criteria. This is of concern to many people, particularly to some of us from British Columbia.
We are concerned about some steps already taken. For example, the Department of Environment spent $1 million on public relations while preparing to announce a few days later that it would cut half the Department. The Government set out to rationalize the shipbuilding industry of Canada, which is an honourable objective, but it chose the president of one of
the major shipbuilding companies to head the rationalization of the shipbuilding industry in Canada. Surely that will not be seen as fair by other shipbuilding companies in the country. It is that kind of behaviour that concerns many of us, and that is why, when we are asked to vote on these Estimates of $116 billion, we are very cautious. We have not seen the kind of leadership and direction that we expected from a Government which was given such an overwhelming mandate by the people of Canada.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I would like to go back to the speech of the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) who stood in this Chamber on behalf of Albertans. Competing in me was a desire to laugh and a kind of churning in my stomach that any Liberal who was in this Chamber after the 1980 election presumes to try to convince anyone in the Province of Alberta that the Liberals give a damn about anyone in that province. I was in this Chamber when the Liberals tried to ram through a Constitution which would have made second-class citizens of all the people in western Canada; in fact, in eight provinces of this country. They kept insisting on it. The Hon. Member who made the speech this morning was doing that. I sat in this Chamber when a Budget and a set of Main Estimates were brought into the House and I rose and said it was a catastrophe for this country and an absolute catastrophe for the people of the Province of Alberta, but the Liberals proceeded to implement that policy with the help of the New Democratic Party.
The Hon. Member talks about people. We moved from a 4 per cent unemployment rate to amost 14 per cent based on a piece of federal policy. It was not because of falling commodity prices around the world. In fact, it was the opposite. It was simply the stubbornness and foolheadedness of the Liberal Party of Canada. Our mental hospitals were full and our prisons were full. The wards in our hospitals were full of battered children and battered wives. We had suicides and heart attacks. And this was all because of a piece of public policy brought into this Chamber by the Liberal Party.
The Hon. Member stands and talks about the bad situation in Alberta today. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is a lot worse now than it was six months ago. Within one year of getting rid of that bunch, the Province of Alberta had taken care of one third of the unemployment problem. Then commodity prices fell on oil and the cumulative effect of drought made the situation very difficult. But there are 31,000 more people working today than in September of 1984 in spite of that reality, in spite of those fallen commodity prices. The employment situation is 16 per cent better than it was in 1984. It was 33 per cent better some six months ago. We are not out of the woods. We still have a higher than average unemployment rate for our province and we are still working on it. But given that rapid drop in commodity prices and its importance to the economy of my province, what is there in the Main Estimates tells us a little bit about the change in attitude of Government which makes that fall slower than it might have been and better for people than it would have been? I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that it is the consistent notion of our Party that all Canadians are equal. There is no such thing as a first class Canadian and a second class Canadian.
I sat in this Chamber through those difficult years when that was a hard concept to hang onto. I mentioned the Constitution and the National Energy Program. If we take a simple thing like job creation, dollars spent by the federal Government for the creation of jobs, the Hon. Member for

June 10, 1986
Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe should remember that in a Liberal Cabinet Minister's riding, the taxpayers of this country put up $586.50 per year for each unemployed person for job creation. But the unemployed in my riding in Alberta were not so lucky. The federal Treasury provided $12 per unemployed person despite the reality that we had an above average unemployment rate and that unemployment rate was created by the Liberal Government. The Liberals created the unemployment, it created the human misery and it gave $586.50 of public money for employment creation to umem-ployed people in a Liberal Cabinet Minister's riding and $12 to each unemployed person in a Conservative Member's riding. That was, that is, and I suggest in my lifetime will always be, the Liberal view of how the world goes round. The Liberals want power for power's sake. They want power for things it gives them personally and there is no coherent public policy view discernible. Whatever sells, do it. If we have to borrow today to get a vote, do it. If we have to pay for it tomorrow and if our children and grandchildren have to pay for it, but it will get us the vote so we can hang onto power, do it. That is the Liberal view.
I hope some of the grass roots Members of that Party over time will be successful in cleaning out the kinds of people who hold those views, because this country needs strong, divergent political Parties with divergent public policy views. We do not need political Parties whose sole reason for being is the procurement and continuation of power. That is what this country has had. That is what has caused us enormous difficulties. It led to separatism in the Province of Quebec. It led to separatism in my province. In the provincial election previous to the last one, the separatists in my province received close to 17 per cent of the vote. With the change of Government it went down to an infinitesimal portion of the vote, because all that the people of western Canada want to be is full and equal participants in this which is probably the finest country in the whole world. They want to be full and equal participants, not second class citizens in their own country. The Liberals would do me a favour if they did not stand up in this Chamber and insult every Albertan by trying to pretend they care a damn about anyone who lives in my province because they do not, they have not and they will not. I look forward to the continuation of my speech after lunch.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as our soccer team disbands and returns home from the World Cup in

Mexico it is appropriate to recognize the tremendous contribution this team has made to Canada's international sporting image.

CANADIAN CYSTIC FIBROSIS FOUNDATION-SUPPORT GIVEN BY OTTAWA ROUGH RIDER'S CLUB
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Canadian Cystic Fibrosis Foundation made history in Ottawa. I, along with hundreds of other businesspersons, participated in the Ottawa Rough Riders' 65 Roses Sports Club Kick-off Luncheon.
The name of the club came from a youngster who was asked why his sister coughed all the time. He could not pronounce "cystic fibrosis" so he said the coughing occurred because his sister had "65 roses". The phrase has since been used across North America as the rallying call in the fight against this dreaded disease.
The Ottawa Rough Riders are the first CFL team to be associated with 65 Roses. An unbelievable 81 memberships of $1,000 were pledged, the first time in the seven-year history of the 57 clubs that a founding meeting generated over 65 members.
Mila Mulroney, Honorary Chairperson of the Canadian Cystic Fibrosis Foundation, Rick Sowieta of the Rough Riders, Mayor Jim Durrell, and Robbie Thompson, the National CF Poster Child, can all be proud of the continued and remarkable generosity of our national capital region.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday in the House the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen), in answer to a question from the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), stated that three years ago when I was Minister of Transport I was involved in a incident in which he claims I was using a Government aircraft for political purposes, along with two of my colleagues. That is simply not the fact.
I want to stand today to correct the record and to say that I was somewhat disturbed by the fact that the Deputy Prime Minister did not have the parliamentary courtesy to stay in the House and clarify that matter when I was here.
History is full of petty tyrants who have used the big lie technique to get their way. Fortunately, history also tells us that petty tyrants are deposed when people see through that big lie. Mr. Speaker, that can happen none too soon in this country when we get rid of the use of that tactic by too many of our government Members and Ministers.

Mr. Speaker, the latest Statistics Canada release on unemployment indicates a new drop in the number of unemployed Canadians in the month of May.
Indeed, the number of unemployed workers in Canada has declined by 102,000 during the past twelve months. Unemployment figures in Quebec for May 1985 were 385,000 as compared with 340,000 last month, a decrease of 45,000. The unemployment rate now stands at 10.6 per cent, the lowest level in six years.
Unfortunately such good news do not always make the headlines, and our Opposition colleagues do not mention them either. Still, the 45,000 men and women who did go back to work last month have nothing but praise for this Government's sound economic policies, and we have every intention of continuing our efforts to fight unemployment.
In my riding of Beauce, Mr. Speaker, the regional media do report this kind of good news.

June 10, 1986

Mr. Speaker, over the past five weeks aboriginal leaders from across Canada have joined forces to work for a new land claim policy. The present policy has failed with only one agreement signed since it was introduced in 1981.
Since recommendations for a new policy will soon go to Cabinet, aboriginal leaders want to meet with members of the Cabinet to express their position. They have not been given this chance. Despite requests for meetings with over 10 cabinet Ministers, only one, the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew), has managed to receive the group. Meetings with four other Ministers have been cancelled in the last two days, while other Ministers have refused to set a time.
Aboriginal peoples want their voices heard before the Government makes up its mind. They object to the present policy that requires them to give up their rights as aboriginal peoples before the Government will sign a land claim agreement. Land claim policy should allow aboriginal people to participate fully in Canadian society. That participation should begin with cabinet members meeting directly with aboriginal leaders to hear their concerns.

Mr. Speaker, under the Challenge 86 Summer Employment/Experience Development program to which $210 million have been allocated, 241 applications have been approved in my riding of Drummond.
Now that these applications have been accepted, 365 jobs will be created in my riding thanks to $461,280 salary grants made by the federal Government, almost $100,000 more than in 1985.
In addition, 1986 is an official census year and we have created 113 jobs for assistant census takers and sector commissioners in my riding. Their total payroll amounts to $150,000.
These projects give students an opportunity to gain practical working experience which will stand them in good stead when they join the labour market in a few years.
I am particularly pleased to be able to participate in job creation for young people in my riding through this program launched by the Conservative Government.

Mr. Speaker, again I would have to stress to the right hon. gentleman that the federal Government is not cutting back on its share of federal moneys which the provinces have to spend for health care because the provinces have jurisdiction in health care. The federal Government's expenditure under the legislation before us, the Budget of the Minister of Finance, is going from $65 billion over the last five years to $90 billion. That is up. That is not down. It is up. Additionally, if the right hon. gentleman takes a look at inflation protection, there is full protection under Bill C-96.
I will agree with the hon. gentleman and all Members of the House that our health care system will also have to adjust. In that respect there is a responsibility of the federal Government and the provincial Governments to come up with a solution collectively, as health care has generally been addressed, to the problem of the aging population and new technologies. I suggest that the EPF is not an answer to the question he asked.

subtopic: LUMBER EXPORTS-POSITION OF UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
LUMBER EXPORTS-POSITION OF UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Yesterday in the House in response to a question the Minister stated that the commitment which the President of the United States, Mr. Reagan, made in a letter he sent to Senator Packwood, in which he expressed support for the efforts of the U.S. lumber industry, was at variance with what the Canadian Government understood to be the conditions under the Quebec Accord.
Is the Minister now saying that the President of the United States says one thing for domestic purposes and another thing to its very close ally and friend, Canada? Is he really saying that there are two different positions on this? Will he clarify his remarks and not leave this very serious charge on the public record?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: LUMBER EXPORTS-POSITION OF UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, of course I am not saying that.

subtopic: LUMBER EXPORTS-POSITION OF UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
speechtext: Now sit down.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: LUMBER EXPORTS-POSITION OF UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
speechtext:
The Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry was quoting a gentleman named Santos as the speaker for the U.S. administration. We always take the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry seriously, however wrong that might be. We have checked with the White House and are advised by
Oral Questions
its spokesman that Santos was wrong and does not speak for the U.S. administration.

subtopic: LUMBER EXPORTS-POSITION OF UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
speechtext: Oh, I see. By letter?

Mr. Speaker, the Minister is mistaken. I was not quoting Mr. Santos. I was quoting the Hon. Joe Clark who is the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He said, as reported at page 14112 of Hansard, that the President might say things for domestic reasons, but they are not in accord with what we had to say.
In his own statement the Minister said that the President made these commitments for his own domestic reasons. Are you now saying that there are two different lines of argument? Will the Minister clarify the record? If not, he will leave a very serious charge against the President of the United States.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Santos will answer the question.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not saying that, and that is clear on the record. The Opposition-
That's what you said yesterday.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: -unable to find any common line themselves, have now begun the practice of quoting, one by one, the 240 million Americans who might have some view on the trade negotiations.
I am quoting you.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: All I can say is that I am pleased we are not dealing with China.
Hear, hear!
Order.
More, more.
Order, please.

subtopic: CLAIM MADE BY U.S. SENATE COMMITTEE OFFICIAL
CLAIM MADE BY U.S. SENATE COMMITTEE OFFICIAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, now that we have had our little joke I will direct a question to the Prime Minister, who likes to indulge in this kind of thing, and see what he says.

subtopic: CLAIM MADE BY U.S. SENATE COMMITTEE OFFICIAL
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: CLAIM MADE BY U.S. SENATE COMMITTEE OFFICIAL
speechtext:
The gentleman referred to by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, Mr. Santos, may not speak for the administration of the United States, but he is a senior counsel to the Senate Finance Committee which has a crucial role in the ultimate trade decision. Has the Prime Minister

June 10, 1986
Oral Questions
checked out with President Reagan or Secretary of State Shultz the claim made by Santos that, no matter what the Department of Commerce decides, President Reagan will intervene at some point to take another whack at Canadian lumber?

subtopic: CLAIM MADE BY U.S. SENATE COMMITTEE OFFICIAL
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, we are guided by the administration and the relationships which necessarily exist. I am sure that there are all kinds of opinions floating around. We cannot check them all out and be held responsible for opinions put out by either Mr. Santos or Bob White.

subtopic: CLAIM MADE BY U.S. SENATE COMMITTEE OFFICIAL
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CLAIM MADE BY U.S. SENATE COMMITTEE OFFICIAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's caucus may think this is funny but more than 25 million Canadians are interested in the well-being of this country. This is not a joke.

subtopic: CLAIM MADE BY U.S. SENATE COMMITTEE OFFICIAL
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Santos, senior counsel to the Finance Committee, said that there has been a private deal made between President Reagan and certain key Senators. The President reversed his commitment to the Prime Minister in terms of the Quebec Accord. Therefore, when the Prime Minister recently wrote his "Dear Ron" letter to the President why did he not make a special appeal for consideration of the legitimate interests of all those Canadians working in the wood products sector?
Mr. Speaker, I must say again, as the Secretary of State indicated, that no one knows Mr. Santos. We have not-
Did he say no one knows him?
He is the senior trade counsel.
That is what I said.
No one knows him?
That is what I said. I do not know him. I have not heard from him and I doubt if I will hear from him again. Am I supposed to be intimate in some way with him?
No, you are supposed to know who he is.
The Secretary of State-
He doesn't know him.
It is nice to hear that Nadia Comaneci is back.
No, please. Does the Prime Minister want to finish his answer, please?
I tried to tell my hon. friend that the response was fully given by the Secretary of State for-
Send Joe in, at least he is funny.

I know the Liberals do not want an answer but I will try to respond to my hon. friend, the Leader of the NDP.
The case concerning the workers in British Columbia was made fully on a number of occasions and will continue to be fully defended by the Secretary of State when he convenes a very important meeting of all interested parties in Vancouver on Friday.

Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister knows, the question is quite serious. It was the Secretary of State for External Affairs who said yesterday that the President of the United States says certain things for domestic purposes and certain other things regarding his commitment to Canada. Mr. Santos, senior counsel to the U.S. Senate Finance Committee, has claimed that President Reagan made a commitment to, in effect, overrule the quasijudicial proceedings now under way. Therefore, will the Prime Minister contact President Reagan and get him to stand by the commitment he made in the Quebec Accord? It is a serious matter.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a serious matter. That is why there has to be some question raised as to why the Opposition is going through the U.S. Government phone book trying to pluck out names and quote them. With respect to Mr. Santos, who was the basis of the continuing CLC case yesterday against the trade talks, we checked with the White House. We thought that perhaps in this unusual circumstance the Leader of the NDP knew something that the rest of the world did not know. The response from the White House is, and I quote: "Santos was wrong and he does not speak for the United States administration". Therefore the NDP is left in the situation where, in order to continue its blind opposition to the trade initiative, it is going to have to invent some other statement from somebody else nobody in this House has heard of.
Hear, hear!
Order, please.
Bye, bye, Ed!

Order, please.
June 10, 1986

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
subsubtopic: USE OF HERCULES AIRCRAFT DURING PRIME MINISTER'S TRAVELS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. It has never been used for the kind of civilian purpose for which the Prime Minister commandeered it. Will he give this House the assurance that the DND Hercules aircraft will never be used again as a pack-horse for the Prime Minister in his attempt to make his version of Bedtime for Bonzol

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: USE OF HERCULES AIRCRAFT DURING PRIME MINISTER'S TRAVELS

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):

Come on!

speechtext: He says, "Come on". The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition I am sure recalls that the same kind of services were used by himself during the last election campaign.

subsubtopic: COST OF UTILIZATION OF HERCULES AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. I would like to know whether he is willing to table today in the House the cost of all the Hercules flights that were made so he could star in some home movies that are nothing but propaganda for the Progressive Conservative Party. Is he prepared to table the cost of those trips in the House?

speakeroldname: Hon. Erik Nielsen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: COST OF UTILIZATION OF HERCULES AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Well, the Hon. Member may be unaware of the fact that the approval with respect to the use of government aircraft is my responsibility. I give her the same answer that I gave to her colleague a moment ago, that the practice of using government aircraft and the PCO technical services was established in 1978 by Prime Minister Trudeau-including video and other such services-and indeed such services were used by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition, the Hon. Member's own Leader, when he was in office.

Mr. Speaker, if the Deputy Prime Minister is not prepared to admit that the video abuse of the Hercules was absolutely unconscionable, I would like to ask the Prime Minister if he does not feel it is passing strange that according to government documents examined today government jets have taken Mr. Mulroney and his family more often to West Palm Beach-
Order.
The government jets have been used more often to go back and forth to West Palm Beach than they have to Baie Comeau.

speechtext:

The number of flights flown have been reduced by 22 per cent. The number of hours flown have been reduced by 23 per cent, and a saving of two and a half million dollars has resulted.
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: USE OF MILITARY AIRCRAFT-WORLD WAR I VETERANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct my question to the Minister of National Defence. A World War I fighter pilot 91 years of age wants to know why he and his fellow World War I airmen were denied by his Ministry, for the first time in Canadian history, the use of military aircraft to enable these few World War I vets to attend their annual reunion in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Erik Nielsen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: USE OF MILITARY AIRCRAFT-WORLD WAR I VETERANS
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman would forward to me particulars of that allegation I will ensure that he has a full and detailed response. speakeroldname: Hon. Erik Nielsen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is absolutely false. The hon. gentleman should know it. He himself, along with his family, has used military aircraft to go from this place to his own home province.

DEVELOPMENT OF HIBERNIA AND TAR SANDS PROJECTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. subtopic: DEVELOPMENT OF HIBERNIA AND TAR SANDS PROJECTS
speechtext:

Member on that, discussions are ongoing with the operator of Hibernia and both levels of government, both our colleagues in the provincial Government in Newfoundland and the Canadian Government. June 10, 1986

taking place to check the various numbers that are involved in the bringing on stream of Hibernia, and the companies now are investigating what is required to bring that onstream. These talks are going on very, very well and we are very confident that Hibernia will be brought onstream.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first of all I must point out to the Hon. Member that this Government has never said it is abandoning security of supply. Quite to the contrary. That is why we are having these discussions. They are ongoing, they are current, and I know they will have a positive result.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT FOR PERSONS OVER FORTY YEARS OF AGE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. With the introduction of the new Canadian Jobs Strategy in one-industry towns where individuals who have worked for a number of years are being laid off due to high-tech or changes in the resource base, will the Minister tell the House her plans for Canadians in the 40 and over age group?

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT FOR PERSONS OVER FORTY YEARS OF AGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Timiskaming for his question with regard to older workers. It is a subject of concern that has been raised by a number of Members in the House. The Canadian Jobs Strategy programs at the moment include some 14,000 people who are in the older worker category. As well, there are specific projects which are directed to them, such as the one in Hamilton, the Citizen's Action Group of Hamilton, that is looking at the problems of older workers in that area. As well, we have Outreach projects directed to those who are over 50. I want to mention as well that in his Budget the Minister of Finance
Oral Questions
allocated some $125 million for an older workers program. These and other initiatives will continue to be taken.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT FOR PERSONS OVER FORTY YEARS OF AGE
speechtext: Order. The Hon. Minister is verging on a statement.

subsubtopic: FUTURE OF DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Right Hon. Prime Minister. Concerns have been expressed recently about the possible demotion of the Department of the Environment to a junior Department, and stripping that Department of responsibilities it now has for the environment. As the person in charge of the Government and Cabinet, will the Prime Minister assure the House that there will be no demotion of the Department of the Environment or stripping away of its responsibilities so that he can allay the widespread concern that exists within the environmental community as a result of that proposal?

subsubtopic: FUTURE OF DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if there are concerns, they would be completely unfounded. I believe it is generally regarded that the Minister of the Environment is doing an exceptional job and reflecting a high priority that the Government gives to all environmental matters.

Will he consider not only not demoting the Department of the Environment but elevating it to the level where environmental decisions, whether they concern agriculture, transport or whatever, are made by the Department of the Environment and not the Departments that deal with the users of particular chemicals or substances that are involved?
Mr. Speaker, it would be hard for this Party to elevate the Department of the Environment because, in our judgment, it is where it ought to be-sky high in our priorities.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT'S LETTER TO PROSPECTIVE REFUGEE STATUS APPLICANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Immigration. I have a copy of a leaked departmental letter that was sent to individuals, including accused murderers and drug traffickers, which states that: "Since you are the subject of an arrest dated on or before May 21, you are eligible for consideration under this review if you declare an intent to claim refugee status." Why did his colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, say in the House yesterday that: "-this review will include no one with regard to criminality."? Why are you
Oral Questions
inviting such individuals to Canada? And why don't you come clean with the facts?

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT'S LETTER TO PROSPECTIVE REFUGEE STATUS APPLICANTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's statement does not do justice to the facts. He was briefed in the standing committee last week regarding the purpose of these letters. Let me reiterate to the Hon. Member, the letter was sent only to those who are subject to an inquiry. The purpose of the letter is only to determine whether those people who are in one way or another in violation of the Immigration Act have any intention to claim refugee status at their inquiry. No one here with any security concerns or health considerations will benefit from this review.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT'S LETTER TO PROSPECTIVE REFUGEE STATUS APPLICANTS
speechtext: Supplementary question through the Chair, please.

Mr. Speaker, it is very clear, and I have documents to prove that drug traffickers, murderers and break-and-enter artists are receiving an invitation to participate in the review. I would like to ask the Minister, since he is trying to separate immigration from refugee claimants, why he is extending an invitation to participate in the review to individuals who have not filed refugee claims and are not refugees. Why does he not deal with the legitimate cases in the 22,000 backlog and not fiddle around with criminals and hard-core individuals?

Mr. Speaker, I would invite the Hon. Member to be part of a positive communication about the intention of this Government which is being widely and positively received. Let me again say to the Hon. Member, and to Hon. Members of this House, that persons illegally in Canada who have evaded removal actions for months or for years are not eligible for the review.
Why did you send them a letter, then? Why send them a letter?
