subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to continue for another 10 minutes on the topic of the Main Estimates. These Main Estimates are similar to the ones which were presented a year ago, but those two sets are completely different from those that were presented to the House for some years in a row. There are several differences which are important to underline.
The most important feature of these Main Estimates is that they are real. There is a reality base to the spending plans of the Government. When the Liberals were in power and we were in opposition we stood up time after time and said that the Main Estimates were not real. Usually some two years later we would see the real numbers from the Public Accounts Committee. We would find that the Government had spent 15 per cent or 20 per cent more than it said it would spend in the Main Estimates. It would receive less revenue than it said it would receive and it would spend more money than it said it would spend. That is how this country got itself into such a financial mess.
I would like to pay public tribute to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) for the accuracy of his last Main Estimates. I anticipate the accuracy of the present Main Estimates. I suspect that when we stand in the House two years from now looking back on this set of Main Estimates we will see that if they err in any way, they will err in terms of over-estimated expenditures as opposed to under-estimated expenditures. That is important for the future of the country.
Within these Main Estimates are estimates for each of the Departments of Government. In the little bit of time I have left I would like to review with the House some positive changes in public policy that form a part of these Estimates. I would like to contrast my view with the view of the members of the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party.
I would like to talk about the issue of unemployment, and in particular youth unemployment. Those of use who have served in this Chamber and who have served on some of the committees of the House have long been aware, in a real sense, of the tragedy that is represented by youth unemployment. We saw the phenomenon grow throughout the 1980s up until 1984. We have seen a significant reduction in those figures since the country had the wisdom to change Governments in 1984. The youth unemployment rate is now falling rather than rising. However, it is still a tragedy. There are far too many young people who cannot obtain that first job which gives them the
experience that leads to a permanent full-time job and, ultimately, to a career.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) announced a change in philosophy soon after she took office. She said that she would take the money which the Chamber votes for employment-creation programs and, in particular, youth employment-creation programs, and try to stretch it so as to encompass more young people. The Minister said that she would try to make that work experience a more positive work experience.
Last summer under the SEED Program, the Minister took roughly the same amount of money that was available in 1984, the last year that the Liberals were in charge, and used it to create over 100,000 jobs. The previous administration created only 65,000 jobs. That is a 50 per cent plus improvement. The characteristics of the jobs were different. First, they were different in terms of wages. On average, wages were higher for those young people. The jobs tended to last 10 per cent longer. The other characteristic with respect to these jobs that was different was that the large majority of them provided career-related work experience.
When one talks about a young person trying to break into the Canadian labour market, the biggest barrier faced is the reality that he or she has no related work experience and therefore no letter of reference from a previous employer. The Minister changed all that. Some 50 per cent more young people were working, most of them in a career-related job in which they could obtain that so important first letter of reference. These letters allow a future long-term employer to see that this young person has met the criteria, knows how to work and has skills related to the type of job being sought. That was a very positive development. Yet when we stand in the Chamber and when we sit in committee we find that both opposition Parties continue to quarrel with the Minister as if there were something wrong with young people obtaining career-related work. It is as if there is something wrong in providing more jobs of longer duration and with better wages with the expenditure of the same amount of money.
Common sense makes us ask, where is the logic in the criticism which we hear in this Chamber day after day? One of the programs affecting youth which the Government decided to cut was Katimavik. There was quite a debate in this Chamber in that respect. There was even a hunger strike in the Senate. I phoned the offices of Katimavik and found out that in 1984-85, the last year for which figures were available, $48 million was devoted to the program. I found out that there were 4,092 young people who started in the program. If one divides the two numbers one into the other one comes up with the figure $11,730 per young person for a nine-month experience. However, only 2,823 young people finished. If one divides that figure into the other one comes up with $17,003 per young person for a nine-month experience. Does it make common sense to spend $2,000 a month on a very small group of young people who are selected essentially at random? These
June 10, 1986

young people do not have special problems, learning difficulties or handicaps. There is nothing indicating that they need something very different from most young people. Through the Katimavik Program, we were spending amounts of money that far exceeded the poverty level for a family of four on each of those young people chosen at random to participate in the program.
That same expenditure of dollars could provide five or six times as many jobs for young people. Those could be career-related jobs and young people could receive their first letters of reference and get started on their careers. I am proud to rise in the House to support the Estimates leading to public policy designed to spend money in a much smarter and better way for the public good.
Mir. Redway: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member commented on youth employment programs and indicated that there has been a good deal of criticism of those programs by the Opposition and others. Some of that criticism has been levelled at student summer employment programs and particularly at the Challenge '86 Program. A good deal of the funding in Challenge '86 is directed partly to the private sector, partly to municipalities and partly to non-profit organizations to provide jobs. This year a shift seems to have taken place and more money is being spent assisting the private sector to provide jobs. As you know, Mr. Speaker, part of the criticism has dealt with the fact that the private sector is able to provide its own money to create jobs for students during the summer and part of the criticism coming from the non-profit sector has been directed at the fact that a lot of the jobs being created for the summer in private industry are not actually career related. As a result, the non-profit sector has been losing funding which it had spent in the past on creating programs for students to get career-related job training for that type of job.
What is the Hon. Member's opinion of this criticism? Does he think it is valid?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for the question. I recognize that the Hon. Member is new to this Chamber and was not here when the former Liberal Government used all the employment-creation programs for virtually one purpose and one purpose only, and that was to help individual Members get re-elected. There was no attempt made to ensure that young people got jobs that were career related and there was not an even distribution of jobs for young people across the country. If a young person happened to live in the riding of a Liberal cabinet Minister, he was a first-class citizen and had a better shot at a job than one who did not live there. If a young person was helping a Liberal cabinet Minister get re-elected, he had an even better shot at the job.
We have made all Canadian young people equal when applying for jobs. We have launched advertising campaigns designed to get prospective employers, private or public, to put
Supply
forward projects that would to the greatest extent possible provide career-related opportunities for young people.
I think we have to acknowledge that within the Canadian labour force, some 85 per cent of jobs are in the private sector. The job picture for young people this summer is that about 35 per cent to 40 per cent of the jobs, depending on the part of the country, are in the private sector. Yet 85 per cent of those young people are likely to end up with jobs in the private sector. I think we have quite a ways to go in trying to provide career-related experience.
Part of the problem with the old program was the pork-barrelling that was the dominant public policy philosophy. I think we have left behind that pork-barrelling philosophy. It is clear in our minds that it is the young people and the reality that they cannot get a first job that is important. Young people have a tough time getting started on a career and our public policy is dominated by the reality that we are helping young people get that first job and that letter of reference so that they may move forward on a career-related path. I support that change in philosophy 1,001 per cent.

speechtext:

If anything, Katimavik provided Canadian youth an opportunity to learn about life and about active involvement in our communities. It provided them an opportunity to learn about the other official language and to serve a period of apprenticeship preceding the seeking and finding of permanent employment. It has been the envy of and admired by a number of Governments in many parts of the western world. June 10, 1986

The Hon. Member for Calgary West complained about the fact that Katimavik cost some $11,000 per youth and he then engaged in quite an elaborate accounting process. The fact remains that these are social costs. These are actually social investments and they are desirable. As you know, Mr. Speaker, there is a high level of unemployment among youth in Canada and any effort that is made by way of Katimavik or any other scheme to assist youth in a transitional way to adapt and integrate into adult society is a good scheme and should be supported.
It is shameful to hear this kind of nonsense coming from government Members who have described Katimavik in those terms and have added insult to injury by describing it as a pork-barrelling employment project. It is also insulting to a study on youth that was conducted by the other Chamber. Among other things, it made the point that if we needed anything, we needed an expanded, reinforced, and perhaps a better Katimavik than the one we have had so far. If it is found that the ratio of investment to benefits or that certain projects were weak, let us improve them and learn from past experience. However, let us not, to use an analogy, throw out the baby with the bath water. We had found a good formula in Katimavik, one which ought to be reinforced rather than denigrated or even thrown away. Up to this point today, the Government has not come forward with an alternative to Katimavik. We are awaiting an answer in that regard. Our youth, particularly those who are unemployed, are expecting a reply from the Government on what it intends to do to fill the vacuum left as a result of the cancellation of Katimavik.
My intervention in this debate is not meant to reply to the nonsense put forward by the Hon. Member for Calgary West. I was glad to hear the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) express a well modulated but nevertheless gently critical approach to the employment program of the Government through Challenge '86. I share his concern. I must say that the way in which he formulated his question indicated that it was well thought out.
It is becoming clear that the Government does not seem to realize that the intention of Challenge '86 is to create jobs at the present time in the private sector with employers who would apparently create those jobs, at the expense of voluntary organizations such as St. John Ambulance. For the benefit of those who may be interested, I refer to a letter which that organization sent to every Member of Parliament, expressing its profound disappointment in the fact that its application was not accepted. It is as if that organization did not create jobs, as if it was an organization which did not provide valuable community activities and experience for young people.
At the present time it would appear that under Challenge '86 the tendency is to ignore the public sector, voluntary agencies, and all those organizations intent upon creating jobs to serve the community. The focus is aimed mostly at jobs in business. In any event, that was not my purpose for rising
today. I am still reacting with some degree of rage to the intervention of the Hon. Member for Calgary West.
I should like to speak about the environment and the amounts in this Bill which will be approved. In particular I should like to refer to $2 million which was approved by the Government. The first $1 million is for an advertising campaign on misfuelling. Mr. Speaker, you are about to hear me talk about misfuelling for the fifth time. I do not envy you, but it is an indication of the stubbornness of the Government. The other $1 million was spent during Environment Week on a number of public relations activities mostly involving songs and balloons, which were not accompanied by decisions, measures, or announcements of substance.
First I will tackle the question of the advertising campaign on misfuelling. I presume the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), who is honouring us with his presence today in the House, must have had a say in approving it. This $1 million measure is aimed at motorists, to discourage them from misfuelling at the pumps. These days there is a tendency at the pumps for people to buy leaded gasoline for cars which are intended to run on unleaded gasoline. In so doing, those purchasers engage in a practice which in the long term ruins the engines of the automobiles they drive. Also, the combustion of that gasoline adds to the level of NOx emissions, in scientific jargon, which find their way into the atmosphere and ultimately add to the acidity of precipitation.
The concern with misfuelling is an understandable one. I commend the Government for being concerned about it. However, where we disagree profoundly is the technique used by the Government in tackling the problem. It feels that a $1 million campaign against misfuelling will deliver the desired results. I contend-and I raised this when we debated second and third reading stages of Bill C-80-that the way to tackle the matter would be for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to revise the federal taxes imposed upon gasoline in such a way that the price at the pumps for unleaded and leaded gasoline would be equal. In my estimation that would be the way to remove the incentive which exists at the present time for some motorists to buy leaded gasoline when they should not buy it. Therefore, it requires a fiscal measure. It requires deliberate action on the part of the Government to remove the market force behind the formulation of the price at the pumps which makes leaded gasoline more attractive.
At this stage, leaded gasoline is 3 cents cheaper than unleaded gasoline, whereas a year ago it was some 2.5 cents cheaper; earlier it was even less. We have seen an increase in the gap between the price of leaded and the price of unleaded gasoline that I can only attribute, in the usual non-partisan manner for which I am known, to the regime of the Progressive Conservative Party. I cannot find any other explanation; perhaps other Members would have a better one.
This brings me back to the necessity of registering with the Government that $1 million in an advertising campaign, as well meant as it may be, will not deliver the goods or achieve the desired result. The desired result will be achieved when the
June 10, 1986

Government, perhaps in co-operation with provincial Governments that also have a say in the formulation of taxes on gasoline, brings about a taxation regime whereby consumers will find the same pricing level between unleaded and leaded gasoline at the pumps.
If my suggestion sounds somewhat outlandish or idealistic, if it sounds as if the Hon. Member for Davenport is on a marginal and tangential kick at the impossible, I should like to allay those fears by saying that three countries have already adopted such a policy. Two countries, Denmark and Austria, offer leaded and unleaded gasoline at the same price. As of April 1 the unheard of happened, namely, Holland took the unusual step of offering unleaded gasoline at a price below that of leaded gasoline for environmental reasons. Environmental reasons are really health reasons or reasons related to our resources, to the damage which is caused in the long term by the acidity of rain. The entire thrust of that fiscal policy in Holland is to make it more attractive for consumers to purchase unleaded gasoline.
Not only has Holland done that, it has also looked at the taxation on new cars, the tax applied by the Dutch Government on the price of cars. It is now weighted in favour of environmentally friendly models and against cars which do not have catalytic converters or other built-in gadgets intended to protect the environment.
This policy thrust is beginning to shape up in certain countries. I bring it to the attention of the Government once again because I think it is using outdated modes of making an impact upon public behaviour by engaging in advertising campaigns. The ads began to appear yesterday. I saw the first one in The Globe and Mail and in Le Devoir. It is a nice ad, in English and in French. Beyond that, I think it will just remain what it is, an ad in the newspaper.
If the Government is serious about the environment, it will have to do something more than just engage in advertising campaigns. It will have to show its political will through a taxation system that favours the purchase of unleaded gasoline and the purchase of cars equipped with converters and other equipment meant to protect the environment. Thus we can reduce the formation of acidic substances which find their way into the atmosphere and fall to earth. These substances get into our forests, our streams and our crops by way of rain and snow precipitation.
The other thrust of my criticism of the Government is the spending of another $1 million, this time not on direct advertising but through activities which took place last week to celebrate Environment Week. You know what they are, Mr. Speaker. They go from balloons to songs and other public relations matters. I would not object if that were accompanied by something of substance. But those measures have been the only measures put forward by the Government to celebrate Environment Week. That is not good enough, for heaven's sake. If the Government had come forward with a number of
Supply
measures intended to restore and strengthen the role of Environment Canada and to heighten environmental interest in the public, I would have said all right, that is good. But we did not hear one word on a number of initiatives that ought to have been addressed one way or the other. I will give a few examples.
There is still silence on the part of the Government on reinstating the Guelph Toxicology Centre, a program cancelled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in November, 1984. Yet we all know that toxic chemicals are the subject of increasing public concern for a number of reasons, best expressed by a number of scientific reports that saw the light of day in 1985 and again in 1986.
There has been no word on the part of the Government about reinforcing the role of the Canadian Wildlife Service which, as you will recall, Mr. Speaker, was cut by 27 per cent in November, 1984 and which performed a very important role in monitoring health effects in wildlife, thus giving us an indication as to the impact on human health over the long term. There has been no restoration of the strength of the Environmental Protection Services in the Department of the Environment which had cuts of several million dollars in 1984.
Parks Canada had its centennial last year. I would have thought Environment Week would have been a good week for a statement on expanding and strengthening our national parks system. There are a number of things waiting to be done. For instance, a marine parks system is ready to go any time the Government wishes to give it the green light. Yet that project has been sitting since 1984. It was ready in 1984 at the time when the election was called. There is silence, and now and then we hear a little peep. There has been no indication of the intentions for Parks Canada by strengthening and expanding the parks system in its second century.
This leads me to another observation. Environment Week lent an opportunity for the Government to give a signal about its intention in the field of scientific research. We should have had a signal that the Government would strengthen and increase subsidies for scientific research, particularly in the field of toxicology, which is, in a way, connected with the Guelph Toxicology Centre but on a broader base. It was interesting two days ago to see the Member from Saskatoon rise under Standing Order 21 sounding his anguish. He said it was all right to cut the deficit but, he said, and it was a big but, let us find money to complete the construction of the Toxicology Centre in Saskatoon. The Member was right, Mr. Speaker. He was expressing a viewpoint shared by a number of people in this House and outside. This nonsense of cutting the deficit at the expense of basic vital public interest has no place in a modern and civilized society and in a modern Government as we consider the Government of Canada to be.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I share the concern, the quite honest concern I know the Hon. Member has, with respect to the environment and its problems. I was most interested in the Hon. Member's comments relating to misfueling and that whole aspect of trying to move people away from leaded gasoline to non-leaded gasoline. The Hon. Member knows very well that he was the Minister of the Environment in the former Government. I know that with his dedication to environmental matters he pressed his colleagues in the former Government to get things done to improve the environment. I would like to know why, with the great interest and the commitment the Hon. Member has to environmental matters, he was unable to get the Government, of which he was a member and in fact was the Minister of the Environment, to commit money to cleaning up the acid rain emissions coming from plants in Ontario and Quebec, specifically, Inco, Noranda and Falcon-bridge. Why was he unable to do that, and yet the present Government has made that commitment and is in the process of doing it? Why was the Hon. Member unable to take steps himself to phase out leaded gasoline and to impose the sorts of taxes he is suggesting here? Why is it that with the dedication he had to the environment he and his Government were unable to do those things when they have been done by the present Government?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext:
The answer is very simple. The present Government has been able to do that which it has done because it found everything ready to implement as a result of two agreements with the provinces. I can even give the Hon. Member the dates of them, if he likes. He need only look at the
clippings of the time to see the confirmation of this in the media. In March, 1985, we made an agreement with the provinces to go ahead without the concurrence of the United States to reduce emissions by non-ferrous metals in all the provinces which are affected by those types of emissions. A public official statement was made in March, 1984. In June, 1984, the first meeting took place to implement that policy. At that time the discussion about the allocation of funds began. Discussion also began at that time on the report of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources on non-ferrous metals with regard to what the allocation would be and what the total cost of the modernization of those industries affected would be.
In that way the wheel was set in motion. When the new Government came into power, it found the wheels turning at a reasonably well-oiled speed. I invite the Hon. Member to look at the newspaper clippings of the day. These things were reported as front page material.
With regard to leaded gasoline, in December, 1983, we introduced a measure to bring lead in gasoline in Canada to the standards adopted by the EPA in the United States at that time. This was five months before the EPA in the United States introduced new standards which were much better. Had I known that the EPA was moving in that direction, perhaps we would have introduced much more stringent levels than the ones we announced in December, 1983.
Finally, with regard to misfueling, I think the Hon. Member is right. More could have been done at that time. My time and energy were spent in the process of setting up the consultation mechanism needed with industry and unions to arrive at a decision as to which new cars and models would be affected by the introduction of catalytic converters. In the summer of 1984 dates were set for consultations which took place in the fall of that year which allowed the present Government to make the announcement affecting 1988 cars.
The Hon. Member will appreciate that things do not happen overnight. They happen as a result of continuous, constructive effort. In that sense history repeats itself. One Government benefits from the work done by the previous Government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to give the Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) an A for effort for trying to explain the lack of any real success in any way during the time that he was Minister of the Environment. It is regrettable. No one questions his desire to have done something, but the reality is that nothing of substance was accomplished.
I have two short comments to make and then one specific question to ask. Particularly with regard to lead, the specific thing he did accomplish was having Gazetted a standard for lead. That was in 1983 and will not come into effect until January of 1987. In a four-year period the Member succeeded in suggesting that we move from .78 grams per litre to .29 grams per litre. The reality is that the level remains at about .44 grams per litre. It took him four years to even think about that, and that was the only thing of substance he was able to
June 10, 1986

accomplish during his tenure in charge of the environment of Canada. That is regrettable.
My second point relates to toxics. The Member will not have a chance to respond if I get into this too much. There is one specific example I can use. The toxicology fund of the Canadian Wildlife Service has received over $700,000 new government dollars since its inception last year. It has received an equal amount from industry and has over 21 programs. That represents $1.5 million worth of new research on behalf of wildlife in Canada. That is an example of specific additional efforts which were not even considered or thought of, and certainly not recognized, by the Member for Davenport.
My specific question is with regard to recycling. This is an example of the rhetoric of the Member for Davenport. The national recycling plan which has been sought by the recycling industry of Canada can do much to help many environmental objectives in Canada. This is something that has been actively discussed and would be part of the municipal action plan which we hope will be announced next October by the Minister responsible for the Canadian resource council and the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan).

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very hard to educate the Parliamentary Secretary with regard to what happened when I was in office. If he likes to engage in little fairy tales, that is his choice. I hope that one day he will grow up and look at the facts as they are rather than as he would like to see them in the distorted optics which seem to characterize his strange mentality.
With regard to his last point, the fact of the matter is that recycling was entirely wiped from the face of the federal political scene in November, 1984. I refer the Parliamentary Secretary to the statement which was made in this House in November, 1984.
With regard to the lack of real progress on lead, the announcement was made in December, 1983, to come into effect in January, 1987. The effect will be to bring the level of lead down from 0.77 to .29. That is a fact and those are the true amounts and sequences of events.
With regard to toxins, it is quite clear that the Government has a guilty conscience. It knows that that is its Achilles' Heel. The Government has taken some pretty nasty measures. It cancelled the Guelph Toxicology Centre. I think it would be politically wise for the Parliamentary Secretary to make a pitch for the resumption of the toxicology centre rather than trying to cover the tracks and creating the impression that no damage has taken place.
I would like to give the Parliamentary Secretay a quick chronology on toxicology. In October, 1984, we received the Niagara River Toxic Committee Report, a very important document. In the months following, the Guelph Toxicology Centre was shelved. In May, 1985, the former Minister of the Environment made a statement in the House about her visiting Washington to meet with Lee Thomas and to bring forward an American plan for full and speedy action on the Niagara
Supply
River. We have heard enough about the former Minister of the Environment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what this debate is all about is the Government Estimates and its request of the House of Commons to spend $116 billion of taxpayers' money. That is a lot of money, even the Pages agree with that. We have to ask whether or not the Government is spending the money properly, whether or not there has been a fair assessment of taxes, too much waste and so on.
I believe we are seeing today a tremendous amount of waste in Government. We have the example of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) spending some $40,000 of taxpayers' money on an airplane to carry a video crew to film him while he was in western Canada. This Hercules aircraft, with a seven-man video crew, two vans, and a seven-man air crew, cost the taxpayers some $40,000. Is it right and proper to spend that kind of money glorifying the man who has the honour to be the Prime Minister of Canada? I say it is wrong and this House should not approve the Estimates as long as the Government of Canada is wasting money in that way.

June 10, 1986
Supply
This is very interesting because it was the Conservative Party that, year in and year out, criticized the former Prime Minister of this country for squandering money. I have been here since 1968 and I have heard speech after speech from the Conservatives about the excesses and extravagances of the Trudeau years. That same Party is now doubling the Prime Minister's staff and paying salaries higher than ever before for that staff as well as the staff of cabinet Ministers. It is the same Party that, as the Government, is using government aircraft to fly the Prime Minister and his family to West Palm Beach, Florida, on non-government business. Yet the Government asks us to approve Estimates totalling $116 billion. It is a waste of taxpayers' money.
[ Translation]
It is really a waste of thousands of dollars in taxpayers' money, Mr. Speaker.

I cannot agree to that kind of waste of money. This same Government came to Parliament one year ago and asked for $1 billion to bail out some banks and their depositors. The majority of that money went to other financial institutions, many of them foreign-owned. At the same time, the Government wanted to cut back on old age pensions. Is that fair? Is that just? Should we approve the Estimates when the Conservative Government is squandering $1 billion, much of it going to wealthy banks in this country and in the U.S? Two years ago the Conservatives criticized the former Government for appointing Donald Macdonald as the head of a commission on taxation to be paid $750 or $800 a day. Now this Conservative Government is paying Simon Reisman, our special negotiator on trade with the U.S., $1,000 a day plus expenses. That is the same Simon Reisman who, when he was asked about the Minister in charge of the Wheat Board, said who is Charlie Mayer? This guy is supposed to be negotiating our trade with the U.S., including agriculture. There is no industry in Canada more important than agriculture and grain farming in western Canada. Yet our chief negotiator does not know who the Minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board is. I think Simon Reisman's vision of this country is about as broad as he can see it from the top of the CN Tower or the Peace Tower. He does not even know the name of the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, yet this Government is paying him $1,000 a day plus expenses to negotiate on behalf of the Government and the people of Canada.
I cannot approve Estimates like this. I do not see how many of the more experienced members of the Conservative Party, my friend from Victoria being one of them, can approve this kind of waste of taxpayers' money. A thousand dollars a day plus expenses for Simon Reisman, and he does not even know who the Minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board is! It is either arrogance or stupidity, or maybe a combination of both. That is one of the problems we have when people who negotiate on behalf of the nation as a whole do not know it exists outside of Toronto and Ottawa. We have this kind of
waste and this kind of tax, tax, tax on ordinary people, and it is for those reasons that I cannot support the Estimates.
At the same time as the Government is paying Mr. Reisman $1,000 a day and bailing out the banks to the tune of $1 billion, the Government is increasing taxes on ordinary citizens in my constituency. I have a letter here from Mr. Tom Seeley and I will read it to the House. He wrote to me on March 30 and told me about how his mother's taxes have been increased. He says:

speechtext:
I have just completed my mother's income tax return and it is obvious to me that the Federal government is picking the pockets of Senior citizens.
My mother is 73 years of age and has a modest income from Old Age Security, Canada Pension Plan, interest income and royalties. Her taxable income in 1984 was $2,164 and in 1985 was $2,222. There was no tax payable in either year.
However the federal tax payable was another matter. Although my mother's taxable income rose by only $58 (approximately 2 per cent) her Federal tax payable rose from $21.00 to $127.00.
This represents a 600 per cent increase in tax payable. Although the return has not yet been checked by the taxation people, I believe this can easily be confirmed by a quick reference to the 1984 and 1985 tax tables.
Although the amount of money is quite small, it is not so small for someone on a limited income. How many of us would stand for a 600 per cent increase in tax payable from one year to the next?
I would appreciate it if you would confront the Government in regard to this inequity on behalf of my mother and all other seniors and low-income Canadians facing this situation.
Yours very truly T. Seeley
Here is a woman with a salary of a little over $2,000 a year, with a tax increase by the federal Government of 600 per cent, an increase in federal tax payable from $21 to $127. Yet at the same time the Prime Minister of Canada will fly, at taxpayers' expense, to holiday in West Palm Beach in Florida, spend $40,000 on a government Hercules and a film crew to film him as he travels throughout western Canada. At the same time the Government will pay Simon Reisman $1,000 a day plus expenses to negotiate when he does not even know who the Minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board is.
Can you expect us to support this kind of waste, this kind of tax, tax, tax, by the Conservative Party of Canada? No way. No wonder in my Province of Saskatchewan, the last time the Conservative Party was popular was back in the 1930s with a guy named Premier Anderson and R. B. Bennett, who was Prime Minister of Canada. They so screwed up the economy that they disappeared for 50 years. The way they are going now history is bound to repeat itself. I hope it does, because what we have now is a Government that taxes the ordinary people of Canada, the poor, the old, and the seniors of this country and gives massive breaks to rich Canadians.
I want to mention one more thing before I sit down and that is the very important sector of agriculture today. In farming today in this country in western Canada we are facing a crisis such as we have not seen since the 1930s. We have tabled in
June 10, 1986

this House last Thursday or Friday a report of a special committee on the price of domestic wheat, a unanimous report that said that we are facing a crisis that is more severe now than we have had since the 1930s. The price of wheat in this country now in 1933 dollars is at the same level as it was in 1933.
With the price of wheat so low I ask why the Government is not spending some money trying to help our farmers. Why do we not have a deficiency payment in this country that would increase farm income by $1.5	billion to	$2 billion a year?What we are seeing instead is	a drop	in	the	initial price of
wheat by 19 per cent, on barley by some 27 per cent.
What we are seeing in the	United	States	is exactly theopposite. There are massive subsidies	in	the	United States
where the American farmer is guaranteed some $6 a bushel. Our farmer is going to get between $3 and $3.50 a bushel depending upon the quality. In Europe the farmers will receive more than $6 a bushel. So I ask why, in the spending of $116 billion by the Government of Canada, we cannot support our farmers by $1.5 billion or $2 billion in terms of deficiency payments. If we do not do that, hundreds and hundreds of prairie farmers are going to go under.
The Americans have massive deficiency payments. The American Farm Bill has subsidies to American agriculture and American agricultural exports of some $52 billion U.S. in the next three years. That is $75 billion Canadian over three years, or $25 billion Canadian each and every year for the next three years. They support their agricultural sector by $25 billion Canadian each and every year. Surely to goodness we should have a deficiency payment in this country which will allow some of our farmers to stay on the land.
The other concern I have goes back to free trade. It goes back to the famous Canadian Mr. Reisman who does not even know the name of the Minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, who is at the public trough being paid over $1,000 a day with expenses. That same gentleman will probably try to negotiate away the Canadian agricultural sector, because free trade will hurt Canadian agriculture.
I have before me a study by the Government of Canada that says just that. It is released by External Affairs. I also have here another study done by the C. D. Howe Institute in this country, which is by no means a progressive or radical research institute. What it is saying in its study is that a free trade agreement on agriculture between the United States and Canada will certainly undermine the Canadian Wheat Board and will destroy our supply management program in dairy products and in poultry in this country. Both these studies point out the fact that things such as the Crow rate benefit under the Canadian transportation system would probably have to disappear, or certainly be radically changed.
If we had a free trade arrangement with the United States in agriculture we would see the disappearance of the poultry industry in this country. Poultry can be produced a lot cheaper in the United States than it can here. A couple of large
Supply
producers in Georgia or Kentucky can supply the entire Canadian market. All they need there is a sun roof to protect them from the sun and that is all. They do not have the same kinds of problems we have with weather. They do not have a turkey marketing board. They do not have a chicken marketing board in the United States. If we had free trade, these agencies would disappear.

Once again it is people like Mrs. Seeley who are making a taxable income of $2,000 a year who are paying money for a welfare bum like Peter Pocklington.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to explain to the House, as well as to the Canadian public, how our Government is going to effectively spend $107 billion, while taking into account that we have $26 billion to pay in interests on debts incurred by our predecessors, the Liberals, and taking also into account the fact that we are going to spend $53 billion for social services. In view, therefore, of the narrow margin within which we must operate, I am pleased today to explain to the House how we will go about it.
We have a supervisory agency called the Treasury Board, and it is specifically at that level that we will make sure that our resources are properly expended, that the moneys made available to Parliament are properly administered. And that is the reason why I shall deal with major initiatives of the Government in that regard, namely, the administration of the treasury.
Before Canadians gave themselves a Conservative Government in September 1984, our leader, who is now Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), outlined the Progressive Conservative platform for a more efficient and practical administration of the affairs of the State. In the document describing the PC approach to administration, he described the steps which would have to be taken to achieve this more practical process and I quote, Mr. Speaker:
One of this Progressive Conservative Government's top priorities will be to effect changes in the administrative techniques and methods of the federal Government to ensure the best possible use of taxpayers' money. The Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board have put together a series of programs to make this objective a reality. One of the initiatives considered is a treasury administration program the purpose of which is to properly manage the funds which Canadians make available to the Government and to us as Members of Parliament. On the face of it, one could assume that the administration of the treasury is an activity which is carried out only by banks, trust funds or credit unions. Yet,
June 10, 1986

each of us administers his or her own treasury, with personal rules for acquiring and disbursing funds. Each of us is eager not to let amounts of money lie idle. Each of us tries to maximize the return on his or her money.
That is the kind of questions that this Government asked itself, and very soon after the September 1984 election, this Government moved to ensure sound management of public monies. That kind of management covers the billing, collecting and depositing of monies due to the Government, the payment of monies due by the Government and the use of Government cash balances.
Government funds are the monies that are paid to, taken out of, and that flow through the treasury. A proper management of public fund is essential because of the extent of Government revenues and expenditures and cash-flow. Funds are well managed when receivables are recovered as soon as possible and payables are only paid on their due dates. Deciding on policies to that end will help reduce that portion of the federal budget that is allotted each year to the payment of interests on the national debt.
In view of the enormous sums of money needed for the efficient running of the Canadian Government, sound management of public funds is essential to an efficient, effective management of the public treasury. The Treasury Board has informed managers in the Public Service that good management of funds was important. In the federal publication Interaction issued in April 1985, this message was sent to them: First, managers should assess their programs for savings to be made by improving the quality of the management of their funds; second, under Government requirements for control and accountability, department plans and proposals will be strictly reviewed with a view to using every opportunity for a better management of funds.
Managers in the Public Service have been encouraged to apply the proven techniques used by the private sector in the area of fund management, to the specific needs of the Government, and to use every opportunity to better manage their funds, whether payable or receivable. Ministers sitting on the Treasury Board have approved a fund management strategy as early as the beginning of 1985, another step to help the Government rapidly and decisively gain control of public expenditures. That strategy, similar to the one used in the private sector, is aimed both at increasing the size and percentage of receivables and reducing the size and percentage of payables. This does not mean that an extra burden will be laid on businesses and invidivuals. The aim is rather to meet the expectencies and requirements of our society and Canadian citizens in the area of the management of public finance.
Improved management procedures for the treasury will be applied to all Government operations, tax revenues and others, payments to suppliers, large capital expenditures, grants, contributions and transfer payments. Proper strategies and processes for each of those items will allow us to save on interest charges, to reduce our borrowing needs and reduce the deficit. In March 1985, the President of the Treasury Board

officially announced that strategy and the steps to be taken for its implementation. Moreover, the Minister of Finance has announced other steps for financial management in his budgets of May 1985 and February 1986. As a whole, those measures will allow savings of $873 million between 1985-86 and 199091.
I should like to point out to this House, Mr. Speaker, the efforts and the outstanding success of the President of the Treasury Board, the Hon. de Cotret, a prominent Quebecer who will make it possible for our Government to save $873 million during that short period. Canadians will thus have avoided an additional debt of $1 billion. We as Tories keep in mind the millions which we have to borrow while the Liberals never thought about it. Mr. Speaker, I am sure all Members will agree that this is an efficient management of the treasury.
Previously, Mr. Speaker, the departments and agencies did not take into account the monetary value of elapsed time, that is lost interest due to anticipated expenditures or late recoveries. In his 1984 annual report, the Auditor General was critical of previous governments who had failed to immediately deposit recovered funds in accounts bearing interest. The Auditor General also noted that bills were often paid before their expiry date. And how often have we heard the Auditor General criticize control procedures of the treasury under the previous Liberal government? Of course, the Auditor General cannot be charged with being partisan.
But this is no longer the case and many initiatives have been taken during the past 18 months. Management of public treasury is not longer outdated. The collection procedure,the treatment and deposit of accounts receivable have been streamlined. So is the method for making payments.
As a taxpayer and Member of Parliament, I expect that Government funds will be managed as cautiously as my own. However, the very cautiousness I am exercising is a reason to appreciate what Machiavelli wrote some 475 year ago. He had this to say: "One must conclude that wise advice from whatever source must necessarily flow from the prudence of the Prince, rather than the Prince's prudence flowing from good advice received".
Then, I will offer no advice on how the Government could still improve its management. I would rather deal with achievements to date, Mr. Speaker. In November 1984, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) announced action to improve the way the system for collecting Government debts was managed. He had this to say, and I quote: "Taxpayers or businesses which pay their debts have the right to expect that we collect from those who can afford to pay but fail to do so." The Government moved to reduce its current level of indebtedness in a way that was both fair and compassionate. This has entailed no harrassment for either individuals or businesses. No coercion was used against those who because of very unfavourable circumstances were not in a position to pay.

June 10, 1986

Such goals have been set to reduce by some $400 million the balance of our fiscal indebtedness. For that also, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Minister of National Revenu (Mr. Mackay) is to be commended. He arranged for those $400 million to be collected. This in turn allowed savings on government borrowings. Those goals were met last year.
Furthermore, Government payments are now made at the right time, that is neither too early nor too late, one rule only, all of which to maximize interest savings. By re-arranging anticipated Government payments, $22 million were saved on the annual budget. The number of bank acounts also was reduced; there were 1,000 under the Liberal administration, we now have 20 such bank accounts. This has meant $20-million savings on administrative costs. Crown Corporations that are not financially independent can no longer draw monies from the Treasury before they need to do so to pay their bills. Because the Government could thereby accumulate interests before paying its bills, $365 million were saved since we used the surpluses accumulated in the coffing of some Crown Corporations. More and more people who deal with the Government reduce our administrative costs by using their credit cards and charging the Government later. Thus we also avoid administrative costs.
The Government has authorized its officials who travel to now use travellers' cheques to cover expenses incurred on public business. The Government has already announced the contract to the En-Route company which will issue travel credit cards to public servants who must travel frequently. Because of this, public servants will not have to request as much in travel advances and to ask for advances as frequently as before, and this will also delay the disbursement of public funds.
Finally, many Departments have implemented their integrated financial management program to increase the potential for savings.
These are important achievements, Mr. Speaker. In addition, the Treasury Board has published a number of circulars to advise public service administrators in their management activities, such as guide lines on the collection of pending accounts, guide lines on the write-off of debts when all collection efforts have failed, guide lines on the scheduling of payments to ensure that they will be made by the expiry date, guide lines on the administrative control of Departments over the loans granted to crown corporations, and guide lines on revenue management and the collection of moneys owed to the Government.
Mr. Speaker, to conclude, I believe that all Hon. Members should applaud the concerted efforts of the Government to implement better expenditure management practices. With the monitoring of revenue collection and treasury movements, the Government is well on its way toward establishing a complete treasury management program. Hon. Members can therefore assure their constituents that the money they have entrusted to the Government is now being managed with optimum efficiency and that all Canadian taxpayers can be assured of the
optimisation of resources. We, parliamentarians, are now managing these resources. It is no longer the responsibility of the Auditor General of Canada, as used to be the case when the Liberals, were overspending and putting us into debt.

Now then, Mr. Speaker, the Small Business Loans Act happens to be one of the best mechanisms to create jobs, but the Government actually goes out of its way to make sure that small business owners will not be tempted to use it.
Mr. Speaker, about ten days ago the Minister said this, and I quote his own words in English:
"Something must be done to increase the survival rate," said the Minister of State for Small Businesses. The Minister himself is saying that something must be done to increase the survival rate. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, budgetary spending will increase 4.4 per cent over the Main Estimates for 1985-86. However, thanks to the additional cutback of $500 million announced in the Budget, the increase is only 3.9 per cent. The growth rate of the Main Estimates is the lowest... perhaps the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier would care to listen ... is the lowest recorded in the last 24 years, Mr. Speaker. Nonstatutory or discretionary spending increased 1.5 per cent. The $500 million cutback has reduced this increase to 0.2 per cent, the same as for the previous year. This is the first time since the immediate post-Korean War period that such a low rate of growth in the Government's operating expenditures has been achieved two years in a row. That is management, Mr. Speaker!
Spending on external defence aid has been increased substantially to honour our international commitments. Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that as a country that is very involved in NATO, we have a duty to maintain our agreements with
June 10, 1986

NATO members, and that is why we have increased our spending on national defence. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, when we increase our spending on national defence, that money is invested here and creates more jobs while saving Canadians money.
Except for these expenditures, discretionary outlays decrease by 2.5 per cent in the Main Estimates, or 4.2 per cent if we take into account the $500 million cut-back. The 5,500 person-years reduction, 2.1 per cent, will mean savings of $150 million in 1986-87. Once the 15,000 person-years decrease is achieved in 1990-91, cumulative savings will amount to $1.5 billion and the annual $500 million savings will continue. These measures, along with others taken over the past 18 months, will cut down projected expenditures and yield additional non-tax revenues of about $6 billion in 1985-86 and $8 billion more in 1986-87.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure you will allow me to focus on some of the highlights which stem directly from our Budget statements. First of all, let me refer to transfer payments to the provinces, territories and municipalities. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Section 36 of the Constitutional Act, 1982, the equalization program is aimed at ensuring that provincial Governments have sufficient revenues to provide reasonably comparable levels of public service within an equally reasonable level of equalization. Equalization payments in Canada are based on a comparison of per capita production or of the yield of provincial standardized tax bases.
Provinces having a less than standard capacity to derive revenues from their taxpayers are entitled to equalization payments to make up the difference. The present equalization formula takes into account practically all sources of revenue of provincial and municipal Governments. The standard is determined by the average fiscal capacity of the five provinces of Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia.
The Main Estimates for 1986-87 provides $5.4 billion for equalization payments. Furthermore, in 1986-87, an additional $65 million will be paid to Manitoba under the Supplementary Equalization Payments Act.
The oldest fiscal transfer payments are the subsidies paid to each province under the terms of Confederation. These payments which include a support subsidy for the provincial legislatures, a per capita subsidy, a subsidy for debt reduction and certain special subsidies, are expected to total $36 million in 1986-1987.
Under reciprocal taxation agreements that came into effect on October 1, 1977, eight provinces have agreed to pay federal sales tax when purchasing goods and services, and the federal Government pays them to compensate for similar provincial taxes and duties payable on such purchases. The four Atlantic provinces and Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and British
Supply
Columbia signed these agreements for which the Main Estimates for 1986-1987 provide the sum of $263 million.
Under the Public Utilities Income Transfer Act, the federal Government pays the provinces 95 per cent of federal income tax collected from private companies that distribute, or produce for the purposes of distributing, electric power, gas and steam to the public. The amount payable in 1986-87 should be about $290 million, including adjustments for previous years.
Mr. Speaker, under agreements with the Territories, the federal Government offers the territorial Governments operating and capital subsidies to help them finance their various programs.
Mr. Speaker, the various highlights of the Main Estimates include the federal contributions for the financing of health care and post-secondary education, under the Established Programs Financing agreements.
Mr. Speaker, under part VI of the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Federal Post-secondary and Health Contributions Act, 1977, the federal Government makes contributions to the funding of insured health services, supplementary health services and post-secondary education. For the cash portion of payments under the program, the Main Estimates for 1986-87 provide for a total of $9.2 billion, including $5.7 billion for insured health services and $2.4 billion for post-secondary education. A further $1.1 billion is provided for the supplementary health services program. The Government also provides $7.5 billion in the form of fiscal transfers, which represent 13.5 individual income tax points and 1 corporate income tax point. Of that amount, $486 million will be transferred to the provinces under the equalization program.
There are also, Mr. Speaker, transfers for specific purposes. To that end, under the Canada Assistance Plan, the federal Government shares equally with the Provinces in the cost of income guarantee and social services. The Main Estimates for 1986-1987 allot $4.1 billion for that purpose. In addition, $400 million will go to Quebec as a fiscal transfer under the opting-out agreements.
Other health and welfare programs are also included, such as work rehabilitation for the handicapped and also programs relating to the health and welfare of Indians. There is also, of course, payments to the Provinces under the prescribed formula for certain other discretionary programs such as the Official Languages programs to education.
The federal Government also agreed with the Provinces and Territories to share the cost it is assuming for legal aid under the Young Offenders Act. I would be remiss, Mr. Speaker, if I did not refer to very important programs such as crop insurance in certain parts of Canada. Also, various transportation programs such as highways, ferry services and a number of other transport services.

Another item of significance is Justice, because there are programs, including federal help to the Provinces for compensating victims of violent crimes and for legal aid in criminal matters.
Mr. Speaker, it is also clear that within the estimates and budget expenditures there is an item that is extremely important-the size of the Public Service.
In the budget of May 23, 1985, the Minister of Finance announced targeted reductions of up to 15,000 person-years in the Public Service coming under the Treasury Board. Those reductions to be spread out over a 5-year period will take effect in 1986-87, and they represent a 2 per cent reduction of the 258,222 person-years indicated in the 1985-86 main estimates and will be carried on at the rate of 1 per cent per year up to 1990-91. In 1986-87, those reductions will reduce expenditures by some $ 150 million to be applied to reducing the deficit and in 1990, when the targeted reduction of 15,000 person-years will be reached, the cumulative savings will be over $1.5 billion so that recurrent annual savings will be about half a billion dollars.
Mr. Speaker, the Government is trying to reduce the size and cost of the permanent Public Service needed to provide federal programs while making sure that essential functions of the Government, such as services dispensed to the public, roads and security services are maintained. Reductions will be achieved by increasing productivity and privatizing some of the federal operations and, if this proves viable, by contracting out other operations. The moves proposed by the Task Force reviewing the programs will go on helpings the Government identify areas which may warrant person-year reductions by reason of program duplication, overlapping or redundancy.
In that context, every possible effort to achieve reductions by attrition have been and will continue to be made. Innovative staff adjustment policies concurred in by public service unions before their implementation in 1985 will help minimize redundancies.
In the Main Estimates for 1986-1987, the Treasury Board approved 252,731 person-years. This is a 5,491 person-year reduction, or 2.13 per cent from the Main Estimates for 19851986. Accordingly, there remains an extra 9,500-odd person-year reduction to be carried out over the next four years.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) has decided to put under separate control, starting in fiscal year 1986-1987, part of the person-years authorized for the RCMP, including members appointed under the RCMP Act. As in the case of military personnel, that section of the RCMP is not subjected to the major acts governing the Public Service, such as the Public Service Employment Act, the Public Service Staff Relations Act, or the Public Service Superannuation Act, and will therefore no longer be included in the person-year base controlled by Treasury Board.
Mr. Speaker, in view of that change, the number of person-years authorized in the Main Estimates for 1986-1987 totals 236,526, excluding the RCMP's 16,205 authorized personyears. In spite of that adjustment, the Government still intends to reach its targeted reduction of 15,000 person-years over the next five years. As previously stated, some 9,500 person-years still have to be dropped from the Public Service and this can be done with a 1 per cent yearly reduction from the 1986-87 base during the forthcoming four years.
The Treasury Board will continue to see that all person-years to be approved for provision in the supplementary estimates for a given financial year but exceeding the targeted reduction are compensated during the same financial year by the removal of authorized person-years elsewhere in the Public Service. As announced by the President of the Treasury Board in his statement made on January 17, 1986, on the impact of the reduction in person-years, steps have been taken to lessen as much as possible the effect of those restrictions on employees. In that respect, it is still considered that no more than 700 employees could be laid off in 1986-87, but every effort is being made to reduce that number to a minimum.
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that we cannot ignore in those excellent main estimates, the improvement in Government management. A number of steps have been taken during the past 18 months to improve management with respect to staff, programs and assets in the Public Service. Those measures reflect not only the present efforts which are made to promote economic renewal and reduce the deficit, but also the commitment of the Government to have productive management in government one of its top priorities. The most tangible evidence of those administrative measures is the substantial reduction of expenditures and the increase in revenues which occurred as a result of the promise to reduce the deficit and to manage more effectively federal programs and agencies.
Finally in a more general way, the various steps taken by the Government to improve its management during the last year and a half will have extensive consequences during the years to come on the development of human and financial resources in the Government as well as on the distribution of resources to federal programs and agencies.
Altogether, these policies will provide a general framework within which public managers will find means and incentives for an economical and efficient management of the taxpayers'money.
On Defence spending, Mr. Speaker, let us look into that comprehensive review of federal programs undertaken by the task force under the Hon. Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) which was mandated to identify overlap areas as well as any possible ways to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of federal programs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Hon. Member for Chambly (Mr. Grise) for such an eloquent speech which was prepared by officials-by the way, he did not seem to quite understand what he was talking about-
The Member congratulates his government for having so successfully managed ... I am sure this does not appear in the notes prepared by the officials-but I would like to know what he thinks of the $40,000 used by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to play the "camera kid", to have his and his family's pictures taken in Florida.
What does he think about his Government's decision to adopt a bill for the purpose of using $1 billion of Canadian taxpayers' money to bail out the depositors of $60,000 or more, while at the same time reducing by $55 millions the indexation of family allowances which benefit middle and low income families.
Moreover, what does he think of his Government's sound management in view of the cost involved in President Reagan's visit to Quebec City and the fact that as far as the Prime Minister was concerned, the sky was the limit! And what about the expenses incurred during the Queen's visit and during the visit of the President of France? What about the expenses incurred by the Prime Minister during his visit to Paris, when he had to grant a scholarship to appear on the front page. And what about the other time in England when he asked to be photographed with Her Majesty, the Queen?
What I would like to know is this: in his opinion do the unfair cuts suffered by the elderly, and all the money given to the rich, represent what he calls sound management? If that is the case, the Member has the right to defend the rich and to crush the poor!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in this debate on the Main Estimates. Today we are considering the $100 billion in the Government's Main Estimates. In fact, I see this as an opportunity to talk about the situation in Quebec. I know the previous speaker talked about good news for Quebec. It may be the Opposition perspective to see the problems that still exist in Quebec's economy, and I think we have a duty to ask, not just in the House but across Canada: How can a Government with 57 Members from Quebec have done so little to restructure and strenghten the economy of a province that is so important to our Confederation?
Mr. Speaker, as you may know, according to the latest polls Quebecers indicate they are so dissatisfied with the performance of the Mulroney Government and their 57 Government Members, that they have dropped the Conservatives to third in the ratings. The Conservatives now have 28 per cent; the New Democrats, Mr. Speaker, for the first time in the history of our party in Quebec, have 30 per cent; and the Liberals, even if they are leading, have been unable to recover the strength they have traditionally had in Quebec, owing to the lack of leadership of their Leader, the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner), and also because of the problem Quebecers still have with the way the Liberals governed when they were in power.
Perhaps I may give an example to show how Quebec compares with the rest of the country. Although unemployment in Quebec has dropped since September 1984, the unemployment rate is still 10.6 per cent, compared with a national average of 9.6 per cent. How does it compare with its neighbour, the province of Ontario, where I come from? In Ontario, the unemployment rate has dropped to 6.9 per cent. Interestingly, Mr. Speaker, in Ontario, the unemployment rate in Toronto Metro is 5.8 per cent, 1 per cent below the provincial average. However, Quebec's largest city, Montreal, has an unemployment rate that continues to hover at 10.7 per cent, with 160,000 unemployed in the metropolitan area and an unemployment rate above the provincial average.
How does Montreal compare with the rest, with the other industrialized cities in central Canada? Well, Mr. Speaker, I mentioned Toronto with 5.8 per cent, Windsor with 7.4 per cent, Hamilton with 5.1 per cent, and even my own City of Ottawa which is experiencing economic difficulties thanks to Government cut-backs and problems at the Technological Institute, the unemployment rate in Ottawa stands at 8.8 per cent.
We have real problems and we are wondering: As mentioned by the Hon. Member who just spoke, is Government management really all that good?
Recently, Mr. Speaker, three weeks ago, some 2,000 shipyard workers of Sorel's Marine Industries marched on Parliament Hill to express their concern about Government mismanagement of the shipbuilding industry, particularly as a result of something which occurred this year. The former Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, Mr. Stevens, the Minister of State (Small Businesses) (Mr. Bissonnette), and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) gave Versatile Vickers Company President Peter Paul Saunders, who comes from Vancouver but happens to be the head of two of the three Quebec shipyards-
They gave Mr. Saunders a mandate to rationalize the shipbuilding industry in the province of Quebec. When Marine Industries workers came to Ottawa, they expressed concern about the letter sent to the Quebec Minister of Industry, Mr. Johnson, in which Mr. Saunders said bluntly that he was given that mandate and that Marine Industries shipyards should be closed. The owner of two of Quebec shipyards proposed the closing of a third shipyard and its conversion to heavy industry. Apparently, there are no shipbuilding contracts.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Small Businesses told them that Mr. Saunders had no mandate from the Government to rationalize the industry. However, a few days later, the Minister of Industry said the opposite. The two Ministers contradicted each other and have not been able to get their act together. We asked the Quebec Minister of Transportation, who is the Acting Minister for that very important department, to withdraw the mandate given to Mr. Saunders because of an obvious conflict of interest, and to consult all parties involved, the three shipyards, as Marine Industries was never

The Quebec Government, the Federal Government, the unions, the Lauzon, Sorel and Montreal East boards of trade should all be consulted. Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your excellent ruling.
I would remind the Hon. Member that Mr. Reismann, who is the ambassador for the negotiations on free trade, receives now a salary of $1,000 a day, or $5,000 a week. That means that in the space of one week, he earns more than two young unemployed Quebecers who are forced to live on welfare payments of $145 a month from the Quebec government. The salary he gets in a week is effectively the equivalent of what is paid to, not two, but three of those young forgotten workers of Quebec who are the victims of an incredible and permanent unemployment. Such are the priorities of this government!
The government of Quebec, Mr. Speaker-and I am referring to its study since those of the federal Government have not been released to the public-found out that about
230,000	jobs in two key industries would be affected by the free trade pact, in a negative way. Now, negative results are
Supply
foreseen in two sectors and finally, positive effects in four sectors for a total of 30,000 jobs. We can ask ourselves, Mr. Speaker: Will the expansion in non-metal mineral products, sport equipment, tiling and aluminum industries and in the wood industry offer enough opportunities for Quebec to offset the negative effects of free trade on the textile and clothing industries, on industrial machinery manufacturing, shoes, printing, jewellery, instrument making, rubber products, electrical products, data processing, primary metal industries, furniture and machinery industries?
Those are the results, Mr. Speaker, those are the industries which will be negatively affected by free trade, by the impact of free trade on the manufacturing economy of Quebec.
We can also ask ourselves whether the Government, during its first 21 months and with its enormous support in Quebec, really cared about the real problems of Quebec. I would say that in many areas the answer is no.
I recall, Mr. Speaker, that on numerous occasions the New Democratic Party has raised the question of the textile and clothing industry, the problem of the loss of employment, as in just four years, since 1981, this industry has lost 13,000 jobs in Quebec alone. Half of the industry is located in Quebec. A secret study done by the Quebec Government shows that free trade will mean the loss of some 30,000 jobs in the textile and clothing industry of that province. I know, Mr. Speaker, that we might be able to make some adjustments, but can we see a way by which free trade in the textile industry, already threatened by imports could not only keep those 30,000 jobs which are in jeopardy, but actually create new employment opportunities? I would say no. Here is one single industry where the loss of jobs will be equivalent to all the gains which will be made in other industries as a result of the free trade agreement proposed by the Government of the Prime Minister.
Are these the changes that Quebecers sought when they ousted the Liberals and helped elect a Conservative Government with a 211 seat majority? It was 212, but there was a slight adjustment recently. Was that the change they had in mind? I don't think so. I believe Quebecers actually wanted a Goverment concerned with economic progress in the whole province of Quebec, in every area of the province, a Government concerned with all the industries threatened by international problems. However, what has the Government been doing for instance with respect to the footwear industry? Almost half of the 8,000 workers, men and women, employed by the footwear industry in Canada are found in Quebec, and their jobs are jeopardized by the removal of quotas.
Mr. Speaker, those quotas were not removed by the previous Liberal Government, but by the Mulroney Government.
Now, did the Government really consider the impact on those jobs in the province of Quebec? Apparently not, as those quotas were removed, Mr. Speaker, with a negative impact on

a major Quebec industry. They began last Fall lifting quotas on some types of footwear.
The survey of textile and clothing industries carried out by the Federal Government has shown that the decline or wiping out of manufacturing activities in medium-sized cities would create a vacuum that would be hard to fill. Yet, almost 80 per cent of all the towns with 10,000 people or more have textile activities, especially in Quebec, Mr. Speaker.
I travelled personally to Sherbrooke, to Magog, and I went through Saint-Jean and other communities in the Richelieu area which depend on the textile and clothing industry-
Since my visit last year, Mr. Speaker, some of the plants I saw have had either to close their doors or else to reduce substantially their workforce because of competition from imports.
Mr. Speaker, what is the Government doing about the textile industry? We have been waiting for a textile policy for one year. We thought that the former Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion had been able to convince the Minister of Finance to accept a policy which would preserve this industry of great importance for Quebec. However, the Minister had to resign because of problems unrelated to the situation in Quebec.
Has his successor given any priority to this matter? Apparently not, since we are now near the end of June. People in the industry no longer know whether they should invest and try to find new markets or continue this contraction of the industry because of their experience of the last few years.
Mr. Speaker, nothing is being done in the shipbuilding industry. The future of a major shipyard has been entrusted to the president of the other two shipyards in Quebec. Without any call for tenders, a SI30 million contract has been given to the Lauzon shipyard. There was no opportunity for others to compete.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member who spoke earlier mentioned the situation in Eastern Montreal. We have to wonder why, if Canadair has to be privatised, the Government did not ensure that the purchaser of Canadair would be a Quebec company. Why did the Government allow Montreal to lose its fourth oil refinery with the closure of Gulf? This brings the total of jobs lost in Eastern Montreal since 1982 to 1,700. Why have over 7,000 jobs been lost in Eastern Montreal since 1982 and why are 5,000 more jobs being threatened?
Mr. Speaker, why did this new Government, which had promised change, do nothing to develop a Canadian purchasing policy which could help companies such as Bombardier, Canadian Steel Wheel and Canadian Steel Foundries, which are all located in Eastern Montreal and which are all threatened in the short or the long term by a shortage of contracts?
Mr. Speaker, how is it that since October, 1985, the Montreal East area has lost approximately 2,400 industrial jobs, and that the Advisory Committee has not yet made
public its recommendations which could start addressing the problem?
Mr. Speaker, how is it that the Treasury Board which is to award contracts by the end of June for the maintenance of its F-18 fleet has done nothing to make sure that these contracts go to Quebec and ensure the survival of the Spar Aerospace industry in that area?
If I ask all these questions, Mr. Speaker, it is because we, in the New Democratic Party, strongly believe that the time has come for a development policy not only for the city of Montreal or the Quebec area, but for all regions in the Province of Quebec.
