speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the spending Estimates of the Governmemt reflect priorities which are dangerously confused and mischievous. The Tories ask, of course, what our priorities are. I suggest that what should concern them, especially because they are the Government, and what should concern us as our highest priority as a nation is the maintenance of our independence, culture and sovereignty. I suggest that what should concern the Government above all is our ability to compete in a very competitive world market where technology and productivity based on research and a highly educated and flexible population are vital. I would suggest that a very high priority for the Government should be to ensure that our future is one of greatness and hope in a countrywhere Canadians from all regions will have the same opportunities.
The Government is spending over $116 billion of taxpayers' money, but in all that spending it is holding back on our research, our future research and on the kind of education we must have to be able to compete in a trade war which goes on throughout the world. The Government is holding back on our youth and on our Canadian heritage and certainly holding back in terms of our future. If some foreign agents were to report on how to undermine and destroy Canada, they could not come up with a better plan than this Government's approach to our youth, our educational system and our research. If the Government had not proven its total incompetence already in a host of areas, one would think we were in the hands of our enemies.
The Conservatives promised before they were elected that they would ensure that these areas of which I am speaking, research, competitiveness and productivity, would be their main concern. They promised they would build on this and it would be our strength. Instead, practically the first thing the Conservatives did upon coming to power, in the name of economy and cutting back on the deficit, was to cut our future. When the Tories were asked by the Canadian Association of University Teachers what their intentions were, if they were elected, with respect to transfers from the federal Government to the provinces, the Tories replied in an official statement: "We are committed to sustaining the current federal financial commitment according to the formula set out in the 1977 agreement". Quite understandably, the Association of University Teachers suspected that politicians might be speaking out of both sides of their mouths and in order to nail them to the wall, the Association asked them a second question: "Does your Conservative Party support the continuation of the established programs financing Act in its present form in so far as it deals with post-secondary education?" The Tories replied: "Yes, we support fully the original 1977 funding formula and the legislation provided for it". In the
spending Estimates we find that the Tories have broken that promise, torn it up into shredded paper. The promise was not worth the paper it was written on. In Bill C-96 the Government proceeded to break that formula it promised solemnly in the two answers I just quoted. Those answers, I might add, came from the Leader of the Conservatives, now the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), through Members of Parliament saying that the Government would not change the formula but would continue to support post-secondary education along the lines of the formula already laid down. The Government broke that promise. It not only broke the promise but what is worse, it broke the agreement established between the federal and provincial Governments which is to expire in March, 1987. The Government not only broke its promise that it would not change the formula but even it broke the agreement with respect to the existing formula made by a previous Government. One would think that members of the Government would be very embarrassed by all that. However, they have explained it away by saying: "We had to do it for the sake of the deficit; we had to cut the deficit".
That is totally misleading the Canadian people because the deficit is not being cut. The cuts are being placed on to the backs of the provinces. It is the provinces which now have to try to make up for the cuts that the federal Government has imposed upon them. Government Members have broken their promises to teachers, students and to the provinces. They have solved their deficit problems by putting them on to the backs of the provinces. That is not a solution; it is just plain cavalier. It is misleading and dishonest.
They also promised that they would uphold the formula for post-secondary education. They made such promises in various speeches. For example, the Hon. Member for Brandon- Souris (Mr. Clark) said that we need more consultation with the provinces and the development of a national education strategy. He said that above all we must understand that this is not the time to reduce in any way the vital resources which the federal Government has been transferring to the provinces. That is the type of speech made by the Prime Minister and members of his Party when they wanted to be elected before the last election. They have broken their promises and their agreements.
I believe it is important for us to understand that not only did they make promises in areas regarding our future and broke them, but they also promised more research and development. One of the major concerns we have as a nation in a competitive and technological age is to have good research and development. At the present time our country is not at the level promised by the Tories; that is, 2.5 per cent of GNP in regard to research and development. Rather, it is around 1.3 per cent, about half of what the Tories promised it would be. No advances are being made in terms of research and development. In fact, we are going backward. While Japan, France, Germany and the United States are at the 2.5 per cent level, Canada is still at the level of 1.3 per cent. Japan is considering
June 10, 1986

pushing its research and development goal up to 8 per cent. We are going in the opposite direction. I say that because the Government promised the universities, the business community and the intellectual community that it would do something about increasing grants to different research councils in Canada. The grants which were promised to be increased were not increased, except at the rate of inflation. That is how the Government has dealt with those boards which give out grants. It was promised that there would be assistance in terms of great increases since, as members of the governing Party said in the election campaign, research and development is essential to the future of Canada. Our educational system has been undermined. Promises made with respect to research have been reneged upon.
Also during the election campaign a great future for our youth was promised. What has been done in terms of that promise? We can see that for the sake of trying to reduce the deficit members of the Government have decided that youth should be the victims on whose backs the deficit must be carried. Presumably the deficit is being cut for the sake of our young people in order that they will not inherit our debts in the future. The future of our youth is being cut back because the Government is cutting back on the deficit. The Tories have closed campus employment offices on many campuses across the country. They have cut back on post-secondary education in terms of what was promised in order to make a viable system of education. Training seats in community colleges have been cut back by some 40 per cent. Katimavik was closed down entirely. Funding which was to go to the Youth Ministry was also cut back. The Ministry has now been shifted to another Department, that of the Department of Employment and Immigration. The Youth Ministry now has virtually no budget and no objectives. The Tories froze the level of student loans, and the list goes on. The Tories have cut back on our youth; they have cut them off at the knees. They are the future of our country and yet the Government has not seen fit to fulfil any of the promises it made to them during the election campaign. The Government also promised to look after research programs outside of universities.
In short, there is grave concern being expressed in the country about the future of our young people. Yet the Tories do not hear it. People have spoken out in every area of the country. The Opposition has spoken out, yet members of the Government have not heard. One person who has spoken out with great effectiveness has been the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, Mr. Justice Brian Dickson. He spoke recently at the University of British Columbia. In his speech he tried to indicate to Canadians that there is a grave problem which faces the educational system. I would like to quote from his speech which was well reported by the media. Of course, as with all these types of speeches, the full text was not covered and some of the most poignant parts have not been given to us. The Chief Justice stated:
Perhaps most significantly, there is a serious, bordering on tragic, lack of funding for universities in Canada today.
Supply
It is the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada who used the word "tragic". I am sure it is a word he would not use lightly, unless it really portrayed the situatuion. In all my travels and in all that I have seen the situation is tragic. The Chief Justice is quite right. His speech continues:
Gordon MacNabb, the Past President of the National Sciences and Engineering Research Council, recently pointed out that of nine member nations of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Develoment (OECD), Canada ranked eighth in total investment in reserach and development, behind even Sweden and the Netherlands. Listen to this description by Dr. Andrew MacKay, the President of Dalhousie University:
"Fiscal restraints have brought student/faculty ratios perilously high at many of our institutions. They have made it nearly impossible for us to bring in bright new minds to teach our students and undertake research. Our libraries are suffering for want of appropriate acquisitions. Most of our scientific, technical and computing equipment for teaching is obsolescent.
Our physical plant is generally in desperate need of repair. And many of us have found it necessary to turn away students we would have previously admitted to our core programs in the arts and sciences because we can no longer do work of satisfactory quality except by limiting numbers."
That is tragic. It is a deplorable situation which exists in the country. It is a situation on which the Government turns its back. It has turned its back on the needs of the universities by changing the formula and by leaving them with even less money than they were sure they would receive in order to be able to supply the necessary education for our young people.
Again, I quote from the speech made by the Chief Justice:
Let me speak first to governments, provincial and federal. Please do not choke off the funding of universities.
That is the plea of the Chief Justice. He went on:
Canada must have good universities with outstanding teachers and world class research facilities. Second-class funding of universities will inevitably lead to second-class teachers, second-class students and, ultimately, a second-class nation.
That is the kind of nation Tories are ready to give to the people of Canada when they come to power. The Chief Justice went on:
It has been said by many people that education is too important to be left to educators. That may be true. But it is also true that education is too important to be left to ministers of finance. Universities desperately require funds to perform their great mission in democratic societies. Governments spend billions of dollars every year on all manner of projects, many worthwhile, others not so worthwhile. In my opinion, money spent on minds will never be money misspent.
When the Chief Justice of Canada has to plead with the Government to provide the necessary funds to keep universities operating, it describes the tragically misplaced priorities of the federal Government. Having served, along with my colleagues, on the task force on post-secondary education and having travelled through the Maritimes, I found that every single university president, the head of every faculty organization and the head of every student union said exactly the same thing as the Chief Justice and Dr. MacKay. This is not simply rhetoric on the part of partisan opposition Members. It is a tragic plight that is facing Canada. Because of the wrong priorities of the conservative, Tory, reactionary Government, we find that our post-secondary educational system is moving

June 10, 1986
Supply
down to a second-class status. That was the evidence that was given by everyone who came before the committee to testify on Bill C-96. Speaker after speaker said the same thing.
The previous Secretary of State, now the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. McLean), at least tried to get the Government to understand the importance of this matter. Before the election, he spoke out over and over again criticizing the Liberal Government for not doing enough. We now find that the new Secretary of State (Mr. Bouchard) is washing his hands of this entire matter and saying that it is a problem for the provincial Governments.
This is the worst Secretary of State the Canadian Parliament have ever seen. He has abdicated federal responsibility for education. He has walked away from it and he is not fighting to give leadership that will ensure that young people are protected and the educational system is given a first-class status. Rather, he is getting rid of his responsibilities by saying that it is a matter of provincial jurisdiction, thus leaving it to them to solve a problem that is a federal responsibility.

Mr. Speaker, as many Hon. Members will know, the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Andre) tabled a statement on our Department's Main Estimates at a meeting of the Standing Committee on National Defence on April 15, 1986. My remarks today will draw upon that statement, but I shall also mention other matters which have transpired since that time.
I remind the House that the central thrust of the Government's defence policy has not changed since it was elected. We remain pledged to meet fully and most effectively our defence commitments. The essence of Canada's security policy for the past 37 years has been firmly rooted in deterrence, defence, arms control, and the peaceful resolution of conflict. We have subscribed to the basic tenets of collective defence which are implanted in the North Atlantic Treaty. Briefly, these tenets centre on faith in the purpose and principles of the United Nations Charter and a desire to live in peace with all peoples and all Governments.
The consistent aim of Canada's security policy for more than three decades has been to maintain world peace and to prevent a war which would endanger Canada. This has been achieved mainly by providing in concert with our allies an effective and incredible deterrent to any aggressive action directed against the West by the Soviet Union and members of the Warsaw Pact.
Because of our inability to defend this vast country alone and to safeguard Canadian interests abroad, we have sought our security through collective defence arrangements. Our military contributions to these collective arrangements, however, were seriously neglected in the 1970s, and they still suffer from that legacy.
When the Government took office, it did so with the determination to increase the effectiveness of Canada's Armed Forces. We undertook to give a higher priority to the needs of the Canadian forces in order that they would have the resources they need to do their job. We stated our intention to strengthen our links with our allies and to honour fully our commitments. In short, we undertook to keep faith with our friends as with ourselves, and this we certainly intend to do.
The defence policy review which the Government has undertaken is nearing completion. The basic policies, which will govern our security and defence arrangements over the next decade and onward to the turn of the century, will be outlined in a White Paper the Government will publish this fall. Whatever changes may be possible in the longer term, our

June 10, 1986

immediate past must be to restore a credible defence posture which meets existing commitments. We must regain the confidence of our allies that Canada will, to quote the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), "no longer be a dollar short and a day late".
When it comes to sharing the defence burden, our increase in European troop strength which is nearing completion was designed to initiate this confidence building process. The task ahead is a formidable one. We must rebuild Canada's credibility as a serious defence partner and give the Armed Forces a sense of direction. To these ends the White Paper will provide a better policy blueprint than has previously been the case with documents of this type. Because of the immensity of the challenge to overcome the deficit, the move from blueprint to effective force structure will require more time than originally planned. Nonetheless, we intend to move forward and to succeed in this endeavour.
As every Hon. Member of the House should readily acknowledge, in preparing the Budget the Government faced a situation requiring stern measures and difficult choices. We have accepted responsibility for both of these challenges. A productive economy and sound fiscal management are essential to the continued well-being and prosperity of the nation. They are also essential to a robust defence effort. To achieve both, the paramount need has been to take decisive action to reduce the deficit and to bring a halt to the ever increasing diversion of our national resources from productive activity to the service of an expanding national debt. We must succeed in this, or continued economic growth and improved defence effort before long will be beyond our means to accomplish.
Since it took office, the Government has given high priority to defence, and it will continue to do so. The Budget demonstrates this. Over the five-year period from 1986 to 1991, the Budget provides a higher level of funding for defence than was planned by the previous Government. The reference levels for the Department of National Defence announced in the Budget are lower than those approved by our predecessors for 1986-87 and 1987-88, but they planned no further growth after 198788.
In contrast, and to the benefit of the Department, the new Budget provides for at least 2 per cent annual growth after 1987 and 1988 thereby exceeding the total funding previously planned for the next five years by an estimated $605 million. This is not nearly as much as it should be but we have stated we will make every effort to improve funding levels further as fiscal and economic circumstances permit.
We are already on record, and I will re-iterate it today, that significant real growth in the defence budget over a number of years is the solution if the forces are to meet their commitments fully and effectively. For the short term, provision for modest growth in defence expenditures at a time when other departmental budgets are being reduced provides evidence of
our firm and positive commitment to an increase in Canada's defence effort.
Let me be more specific. The defence budget will grow in real terms, after the effects of national inflation are taken into account, by 2.75 per cent in 1986-87 and thereafter at 2 per cent per year. The result of such action is that the defence budget will increase by approximately $3.2 billion over the period 1986-87 through 1990-1991. Capital expenditure will rise to well over $3 billion over the next five years. However, I would be less than candid if I did not note that a significant part of this increase will be needed to offset defence inflation, which is substantially higher than the rate of national inflation. Even so, we do not intend to cancel any major projects that are essential to meeting our commitments. Some will have to proceed at a slower pace, others may have to be reduced, but the over-all program for the re-equipment of the Canadian Forces will still move forward.
For example, the CF-18 project is now nearing completion. Naval modernization is well under way and has received added impetus with the recent announcement of the $1.2 billion TRUMP project. Army re-equipment is proceeding at a lesser pace but the decision to proceed with the low level air defence project, albeit at a slower rate of implementation than we would wish, will still overcome one of the most serious operational deficiencies in our European based forces.
The size of the regular force will continue to increase and the strengthening of our forces in Europe will be completed. We shall also give close attention to upgrading the reserve force. In the short term, funds from the readiness and sustainment increment will be extensively utilized to provide tangible improvements in this area. In the fall of this year we will exercise, for the first time, the deployment of the full air-sea transportable brigade group which Canada has committed to the defence of northern Norway. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) has already informed the House, units of our Maritime forces will conduct exercises in our eastern Arctic waters during the summer months. More generally, operational trading activities will be maintained at a level which will ensure the continued readiness of our forces and their full participation within the alliance.
The 1986-87 Department of National Defence estimate of $9.96 billion represents 9.3 per cent of the federal Budget. This compares with 9.2 per cent last fiscal year. The Department's share of the federal budget is the third largest in size after the Department of Finance at 30.7 per cent and the Department of Health and Welfare at 26.4 per cent.
The 1986-87 estimates show an increase for defence of $572 million over the 1985-86 estimates. This represents an increase of 6.1 per cent and, as I noted earlier, permits a real growth of 2.75 per cent for the coming year based on the current projection of the national inflation rate for 1986-87.
The Canadian Forces must never again be allowed to fall into the state of disrepair which undermined Canada's credibility as a responsible defence partner in the 1970s. These
June 10, 1986

budgetary allocations will not allow us to do everything that the Government considers to be necessary for defence. The primary objective of our Government is to set the nation's financial house in order and to secure Canada's economic future. It is also vitally important that Canada play its full part in securing peace with freedom in concert with our allies. These two objectives are linked. I am confident that the course we have charted in economic policy will succeed. With success will come the capacity to do what must be done for Canada to bear its fair share of the burden and responsibilities of alliance, to strengthen its voice in the councils of nations and thereby contribute to common security and well-being.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are involved this evening in debate on the motion to concur in the Estimates. I appreciate the opportunity to say something on this thirteenth and final allotted day for the supply period. I want to deal particularly this evening with the Estimates
providing for the Government's implementation of multicultur-alism policy, for expenditures which are to be carried out particularly through the multiculturalism sector of the Department of the Secretary of State. These expenditures are the responsibility of the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Jelinek). In considering these Estimates I want to say something about the inability which members of the Opposition have experienced to consider those Estimates at any length in committee.
The process of considering Estimates is sometimes rather curious. A good deal of it can, I fear, be a matter of pro forma action in which a Government with a great majority approves the spending and calls upon the House of Commons to give its support to enormous expnditures during the year, which expenditures will exceed $100 billion. The possibility of considering these expenditures in any detail is fairly limited in the House. The consideration can sometimes become almost perfunctory.
The Opposition usually has a sense of inadequate action by the Government. What is sought then is not any reduction in expenditures or disagreement with what is put forward as such, but rather the possibility of adding to the amounts that will be spent. Clearly in the case of multiculturalism expenditures, which amount to a little more than $24 million, the desire to have more resources devoted to this important area of social, cultural and economic action in the country is something which I want to advocate very strongly.
The main opportunity for the Opposition to make its feeling known is frequently, particularly in the provincial houses, to propose a motion to reduce the Minister's salary to $1. Such a motion strikes me as quite appropriate in the case of the Minister of State for Multiculturalism. He is, of course, a double Minister of State with responsibility for fitness and amateur sport as well as multiculturalism. I suppose he could manage if the multiculturalism portion were reduced to only $1.
The reason I suggest that one would like to reduce his salary to only $1 is because the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism has not given my colleague, the critic for the Official Opposition on multiculturalism, and myself the opportunity we wanted to deal with the Minister on his Estimates, and to clarify the policy of the Government and where the expenditures will be focused during the current fiscal year. Through this process we will satisfy ourselves that the Government is dealing properly with the multicultural policy for which it is responsible.
I recognize that some of the difficulty I am alluding to occurred thanks to the recent establishment of this committee and the need to arrive at a reference and order which would ensure that this part of the Estimates of the Department of the Secretary of State was assigned to the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism rather than the committee responsible for the Department of the Secretary of State.
June 10, 1986

I suggest, however, that some of it involved an order that was arrived at in the last part of May which gave the responsibility to the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism and led to the cancellation of a meeting on May 27. I expected the Minister to appear then so we could carefully consider with him his spending plans for the year. The fact that the committee meeting was cancelled and no meeting was laid on to consider the matter is the basic procedural and parliamentary reason for my objection to passage of the Estimates. It is also the reason for my suggestion that it would be appropriate to reduce the Minister's salary to $ 1.
I should perhaps say that we are hoping to have the Minister appear before us next week. I hope his office will be attentive to my comments this evening and that they will come better prepared for that encounter than they would otherwise. If we are going to have a meeting with the Minister, let it be a fruitful meeting where we are provided details on the application of policy and the division of the Estimates for his sector. Let us have that kind of detail so we can have a really useful meeting. It will be a meeting clearly after the fact in parliamentary terms, given our consideration of the Estimates today and the votes we face later this evening. However, it would at least give us in the Opposition the opportunity to fulfil our constitutional responsibility of scrutinizing closely the spending plans of the Minister.
To expand on the larger issue, the difficulty we face is that the multiculturalism policy this Government is following has been brought into question over the last number of months. Neither has there been any clear statement at any length, with spending details attached, to which one could respond or with which one could deal critically in considering the appropriateness of the Minister's decisions. This situation of uncertainty which the Minister has created by his actions over the last number of months is why I want to take a look back toward the beginning of this Government's mandate in the fall of 1984, and scan some of the suggestions I had the opportunity to make for clarifying the Government's policy and establishing structure in the multicultural area.
I can look back as far as the month of November, 1984 when I had the opportunity in a statement under Standing Order 21 to emphasize the importance of a separate department of multiculturalism. In concluding my observations that afternoon I said that:
The Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Murta) is reportedly engaged in consultations with ethnic groups to consider the direction of Canada's multicultural policy. I hope these consultations create a better result than the previous Government's multiculturalism Bill of last June. Let the Government show its good will by honouring at least one campaign promise, one that holds an enormous symbolic importance for thousands of Canadians.
To see a department established and have its policy clarified is something we have waited for over many months. I used the occasion of Private Members' hour on September 9, 1985 to expand on this topic. My motion for the creation of the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism, as well as a distinct department of multiculturalism, had found fulfilment as far as the committee was concerned as of last June. However, as far
Supply
as the department was concerned we had some indications in August of 1985 that the Government might be considering it. Here we are now nine months later and we are still waiting. The observations I made that particular afternoon are still waiting for fulfilment. As a matter of fact, if the Minister had a mandate in August of 1985 to consider what sort of administrative rearrangements would be advisable if the Department of Multiculturalism were to be created, we have not seen any indication of it since then. It has fallen like a stone into a pond. There were some small ripples but now the pond has gone limpid again.
We might have expected as well a White Paper on multiculturalism which would spell out the Government's policy. Again I have used occasions over the past months to say something about that. In the same Private Members' hour on September 9, 1985 I spoke as follows:
The Government is at work on a White Paper dealing with multiculturalism. That White Paper has been expected for some time and is likely to appear early in the new year, one gathers. Presumably it will be followed by a Multiculturalism Act, which has long been hoped for by persons active in ethnocultural affairs across the country. This suggests that the deliberations of Government may well be involved with this question.
The "question" being the establishment of a department. That was the beginning of September, 1985. Where are we now? We are nearing the middle of June in the second part of the first session and we have not seen any action on a White Paper. We have not been apprised of what sort of multiculturalism act might be arrived at. Obviously we have had none of the basics needed to create a department.
When I questioned the Minister about this last November, he suggested he would be meeting with the new Standing Committee on Multiculturalism in a week or two. That part of it was true enough. He then went on to say at that time we would be able to discuss at length the details of an Act and a White Paper.
The deliberations with the Minister when he did meet with us later in November did not provide any guidance as to what the Government might be thinking about concerning a White Paper. There was certainly nothing of the White Paper itself in evidence and we certainly did not get any clear sense of what sort of Act we might get. Sadly enough, groups from all across the country who have provided input of all sorts towards the drafting of an Act, as well as suggestions for the structure of the department, continue to wait. By the time in April that I took up the Minister's inadequate responses to my questions of last November, it was quite clear that not only did we not have a White Paper or an Act to consider, there was no department being created. What had occurred in the meantime were suggestions for dramatic changes in policy.
The Minister suggested that he was already implementing certain changes, though he talked about people, including Members of Parliament having an opportunity to debate these changes. He also suggested quite clearly that he was involved in implementing changes without regard, other than for his

June 10, 1986
Supply
cabinet colleagues, to what the people of Canada might think. Perhaps I am a shade too strong on that. Let me review what happened in the interim.
Earlier this winter the Government tabled the various volumes on the Nielsen Task Force on Program Review. In that review there were a number of aspects that touched on the multiculturalism policies and practices of the Government. I note that in the central recommendations, the options which the task force had recommended to it by the study team, the first two items, which very quickly aroused enormous unease were the following:
1.	In helping to overcome barriers to full participation in society and increasing the recognition of the contribution of ethnic groups to Canadian society, the Multiculturalism Branch activities and programs should concentrate on facilitating cultural integration.
In that fateful last word was a suggestion to which ethnocultural organizations and persons concerned about them have been reacting ever since. Item 2 says the following:
2.	Phase out federal funding for organizations and projects aimed at cultural retention and that they be assumed by the communities themselves, the provinces, and the municipalities or other federal programs.
There in two suggestions, end support for cultural retention and encourage cultural integration, was a fairly clear cut statement for an assimilationist policy to be followed by this Government.
When the leaders of the study team appeared before the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism this morning it was clear that a consensus had been arrived at among that group of Conservative advisers to government. They conceded that another group might have come out with different conclusions with the same evidence. They approached with a bias, a bias toward assimilation, and they came out with these recommendations.
What did the Minister do about these things? Here is where the fat is really in the fire. In an interview which the Minister gave about March 6 he announced:
-that he has been working on a "totally new multiculturalism policy" aimed at bringing ethnic minorities out of "ethno-cultural corners" and into the economic mainstream of Canada.
The policy was in the final stages of preparation for Cabinet consideration, according to this report in The Globe and Mail. Some may say that this is really what you should be concerned about as far as the White Paper is concerned.
This was not a policy statement for presentation to the House or for publication to Canadians inviting reaction. The Minister said he was developing a "totally new multiculturalism policy", and it was in the final stages of preparation for Cabinet consideration. He went on to say the following:
It will include involving ethnic minorities more in business-
That was an emphasis on which he was to be acting very quickly. On the other hand, he was going be cut grants to certain ethnic organizations. He went on to say the following:
We are in the process of reviewing the whole funding and granting procedures in line with the development of the new policy.
He said there is not going to be additional money for multiculturalism.
It's going to be redirection of existing funds.
That would be basic to the policy shift.
There's no doubt some organizations are going to be cut out.
He would not identify for the reporter which ethnic organizations he planned to stop helping. He did say he had begun implementing the policy.
About five weeks after this particular interview, there was the Multiculturalism Means Business conference in Toronto, costing the sector a couple of hundred thousands of dollars in order to run it. It clearly involved just that kind of redirection of existing funding. Let the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Bissonnette) undertake this rather than having this sector lose money from those activities in order to pursue the Minister's new ideas.
That particular interview and the publication of the Nielsen task force documents and the Ministers' conference in Toronto, all of them together, have suggested to ethnocultural groups across the country and their leaders that the Government is shifting policy. There is no opportunity to respond to it except in the way of the writing of letters, the statements in the media and so on. Parliament has not been given an opportunity to debate this. There is no White Paper before us and no Act has appeared. When we sought the opportunity in committee to deal with this at the appropriate time, it was taken from us.
The Minister did, of course, appear at a meeting in May and he confused the matter further by denying the things that had been published in that particular interview. I have made a note of some of the things the Minister said in response to my questions. First, there was the matter of whether organizations would lose funding. He began by stating the principle again:
-if there is an ethno-cultural organization in Canada, which is not contributing to the well being of the community in any way, shape or form-
It should not receive funding. Then he said very quickly:
To date we have not found such an organization. Every organization that is being funded by the Government of Canada appears to be contributing to the well being of its community and therefore will continue to receive funding.
I wonder what sort of serious study was involved. The Minister opened the possibility that organizations would not measure up. Now he is saying very hastily that they had not found any such organizations. Given what the Nielsen task force said about the lack of evaluations in this particular sector, I doubt he had any more information at hand to justify saying that.
Then there was the precise question of whether there was going to be more money or a redirection of money. He had said there would not be, that there would have to be redirection. The Minister complicated the matter completely by saying the following:
I read the story at that time. I forget the wording of it, but-and I am not trying to backtrack or put the blame on anybody else-there were several statements in that story that were taken out of context. Where I said there will be
June 10, 1986

no new funds for the time being is within the context of our cultural retention and promotion.
But certainly if we are going to move into new directions, such as the area of education or the area of multiculturalism and business, or other areas, then it is my intention, and always has been, to go before Cabinet, first to get the approval of that direction, and second, to get the necessary resources.
That is admirable. That is what one would expect, but he had not said that earlier. The basic questions remain: What is the multiculturalism policy of this Government? What are the directions it intends to take? What sort of reorganization will occur in the sector? Where is the study which the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. McLean) was authorized to undertake last August? Has it been completed? Is the Minister of State for Immigration making recommendations for the establishment of a department? What will its structure be? What sorts of resources will be available to the Minister of State for Multiculturalism or, as he would become, simply the Minister of Multiculturalism with a full-fledged department? What sorts of resources will he have? What kinds of policy directions will be funded adequately? Where will there be standstill or fallback?
Those questions cry out for an answer. Those are the kinds of questions we wanted to ask the Minister in committee while we were considering his estimates. This evening I am speaking to this question and suggesting that the appropriate action to take regarding this Minister would be to reduce his salary to $1 and demand that the Government give us the White Paper, set forth policy and give us an Act to debate so we could make the kind of progress in multiculturalism this country wants. That is what needs to be done.
I look to the Government and demand that it act along the lines that its policy envisaged during the election campaign. It has been almost two years since the election. The Government is half way through its mandate with precious little done, except confusing Canadians generally, particularly those concerned about the the ethnocultural communities.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have an audience.
First of all, I think we should remember that this debate concerns a motion inviting the House to concur in the Main Estimates tabled by the President of the Treasury Board on February 27. I think our listeners and those who are going to read these proceedings should know that a fairly substantial amount is involved, namely 116 billion 740 million dollars. This is not peanuts, Mr. Speaker. This money is to be spent on governing this country and administering the programs of our
Supply
various departments, and will also be used to pay for Government spending.
We were informed today that the Government is trying to be more effective in its programs and more efficient in the way it implements these programs. We all agree, Mr. Speaker, it is a good thing this Government's aim is to be efficient and effective. Mr. Speaker, the fact remains that among the Estimates to be found in the blue book, there are many expenditures that raise a number of questions for the Members of this House, and since they would like to put these to the various Ministers, we hope we will soon be able to go into Committee of the Whole so that we can question the Ministers in the House and find out how they intend to proceed with these enormous sums of money, this $ 116 billion they want to spend.
Mr. Speaker, I am going to take up the case of our federal public servants, because in my riding and the area I represent, the Public Service is important for jobs and careers. We are now in the month of June, which is graduation time at our universities and high schools, and I know there are many young and capable university graduates who are looking for jobs, and who normally would look to the federal Government for a job in the National Capital Region.
Mr. Speaker, we know that in the NCR, Conservatives have been hitting these jobs for a number of years. In 1979, they had a policy for cutting Public Service employment. They were going to cut 60,000 jobs. We know that the President of the Treasury Board, Mr. Stevens, said: I am going to cut 60,000 jobs.
Indeed they were eventually defeated and then took office again and did not forget their project to cut and slash personnel. They took a more discreet approach, they were more ... I will not use the word "deceitful" but they went about it more slowly. They said they had cut 15,000 jobs.
As a matter of fact, we know that 5,500 positions will disappear this year, a quarter of them-27 per cent to be precise-in the National Capital Region. This means jobs, it means that families will have to revise their budget and even in some cases consider new careers to meet the requirements of a Government which, in principle, says it wants to be more effective and more efficient.
To achieve that, Mr. Speaker, they decided to cut staff and slow down economic activities in the National Capital Region. And when I say that I mean that the major employer has reduced economic activities in the region by a substantial margin, and later on I will explain to the House how these cutbacks affect the region.
In May 1985 as you may recall, and I will give the figures, the Mulroney Government announced a reduction of 15,000 jobs in the public service over the following five years.
As I said a moment ago, the federal Government is the main employer in the National Capital Region and accounts for

June 10, 1986
Supply
nearly 28 to 30 per cent of all economic activities in the region. It is therefore very important.
After the cut-backs were announced, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) tabled a document to propose further cut-backs of about $500 million and a hiring freeze. On top of that, we were told that cut-backs similar to the 15,000 public service jobs would probably be made in Crown corporations and other administrations not directly related to the Treasury Board. So if we add up the 15,000 jobs which have been cut and the 15,000-it isn't I who said it, it's in the Budget papers-15,000 similar jobs in Crown corporations, we get
30,000,	and if we also take into account the $500 million in programs which will be terminated, it is not difficult to extrapolate, Mr. Speaker, and conclude that all this is going to have a rather significant and probably negative impact on job creation in the National Capital Region. Let me explain: I am not an economist, but economists always say that a job in the public sector will create a job and a half in the private sector. As I was saying earlier, this is therefore an important proportion. If you take 30,000 jobs in the federal public sector, and if you multiply that by the 1.5 job creation factor in the private sector, we could end up with 45,000 jobs being directly or indirectly affected over the next five years by these government cuts.
It could have, therefore, a rather significant impact and I want to serve notice to my constituents that we will have steps to try and stop that. The Government says: Dont worry! We are going to diversify the local economy. Mr. Speaker, we have already tried to diversify in the area of science and technology; we have tried to set up in the region a high tech computer industry. This worked rather well. I know that we have here the so-called Ottawa Silicone Valley and there were a series of private initiatives supported by the Government to try and diversify the economy and make jobs in the private sector as interesting, if not more so as those in the public sector.
We have not yet been very lucky in the high tech industry, but I am still hoping for the day when we will be able to rely more on it than on the public sector.
From last November to today, Mr. Speaker, there have been fairly significant cuts in the personnel of the Public Service. What I mean to say is that the House should realize that these cuts will become effective on April 1st of this year. The 15,000 fewer jobs will therefore take effect on April 1, 1986. The cuts ordered by the President of the Treasury Board from the budgets of various departments over the past few months have been rather harsh for some people.
Although I do not always trust statistics for evidence, statistical data indicate that there are now in the region 3,000 more unemployed than there were at the same time last year. Three thousand more jobless in the Ottawa area than there were in 1985, that's a fairly large number of people looking for jobs and obviously not getting any from the main employer, the Government, jobs that would meet their career expectations.
Mr. Speaker, to avoid being told I am totally obsessed by this employment cut-back in the Public Service, I want to point out to Hon. Members that in my riding of Ottawa- Vanier the federal Government is not, contrary to what many people think, the number one employer. It is so for the whole National Capital area, but in the riding of Ottawa-Vanier, a riding relying largely on service industries, the education and health sectors are the big employers.
I think of universities for example which employ about
3,000	people in my riding. To have 3,000 more unemployed in a year is as if the University of Ottawa had been abolished, as if the 3,000 jobs provided by the university had been eliminated. That is the impact. I am trying to quantify this. We have a large number of jobs in the health sector. There are several hospitals in my riding. More than 4,000 people are working in that sector in my riding. That too is in the service sector, Mr. Speaker.
In the education sector, in addition to the university, my riding has a post-secondary college and also several elementary and secondary schools.
Government policies have a snowballing effect that is puzzling a lot of people.
Hotels, local trade, businesses, retail sales, housing starts, sales of houses, all of these give a fairly good indication of the economic well-being of the region. And if you take hotels, for instance, you might think that with an attractive dollar and the potential attraction of our region for American tourists, tourism in Ottawa, in the National Capital Region, should be expanding and our hotels would be able to welcome a lot more people. However, that is not the case! Hotels are presently going through hard times. They have an occupancy rate which is very low, and I am told this is because of Government cuts. I have no comments on that, because I think tourism... but that is what I am told. I am told that it is because of the cuts. I am told that it is because there is no lobbying. I am not saying that I endorse those things. I am just saying that I was told that.
I do not know if it is true. I have no proof of that. But what I know is that hotel managers are saying that the tourist trade is depressed in the National Capital Region.
Housing starts are down, Mr. Speaker. Houses for sale ... just travel through my constituency, and you will see that there are many houses for sale. People are worried. The real estate market is somewhat undecided presently because people are concerned with ensuring, with reinforcing their economic position, and they want to sell houses which carry heavy mortgages.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) who is here with us and is a man who has good ideas sometimes, not all the time, but sometimes, has announced that the freeze was being lifted and that the Government was going to hire people again in its departments.
June 10,1986

I hope this initiative will be recognized by officials as a means of attracting young people, recruiting young people. I think it is time that people should be told that they can make a career for themselves in the Government and that the Government encourages university graduates to apply for positions with the federal Government. We need those professionals. We need those young people and we need that recovery, and I think the Government made the right move in deciding to lift that freeze a few days from now and start hiring people again.
I believe it is a positive step at this time of the year, when a lot of young people are looking for a job.
I therefore congratulate the President of the Treasury Board for lifting that freeze and recognizing the present need in our region to hire young students, young graduates who are looking for jobs.
Mr. Speaker, as the President of the Treasury Board is with us, I would like to go back to the bonus that was offered to the employees in his Department. This morning, I started to ask him what eligibility criteria were used for that performance or productivity bonus, because I tend to be a little suspicious when a program is applied or announced but the criteria to be used for that program are not made public.
In the last few months, I have tried to find out, how one could maintain-and I am not the one who says so but the Minister himself-that 4,000 senior managers or high officials could get productivity bonuses if they attained the Government's expense reduction goals. How such a program could be administered may be a bit difficult to understand for some people. That is why this morning 1 asked the Minister if he could give us before the end of the day the criteria for this program. He did not answer my question. He told me it would be done within a few days and that the particulars of the program would be made known before the end of the month, I think.
I have talked to a few managers in the Public Service and they are not so sure they want to have this money, basically because this kind of productivity incentive can be counterproductive. The managers, of course, whose responsibility it is and who receive higher salaries, have been told that if they reach the Government's objectives in cutting into programs and possibly reducing expenditures, they will receive a premium. Why this reward? Why give incentives to people who are already being paid to do a good job and who receive higher salaries to effectively manage programs in an efficient manner? I do not understand and that is why I ask.
I am not being naive when I ask the question. I have done research. I have looked at several jurisdictions. In Washington there is a program of this sort and there are pros and cons. There are arguments for and against incentive programs. I can quote a few arguments against incentives from a document entitled "Public Personnel Management" which states that
Supply
incentives circumvent the purposes of non-profit organizations. In a sense, incentives act like profit sharing and such action is against the basic concept of non-profit organizations. In the private sector, incentives are generally based on some level of productivity or output and are tied to revenue. In a non-profit organization, earning money is not considered the basic objective. Because of this, non-profit organizations have naturally been more concerned with the services they offer than anything else, including money.
The document goes on to explain that in the legislature of the State of Washington, a Bill passed on March 3, 1982, rewards certain people but it is based on budgetary Estimates, based on sums of money which are known to be lumped for the purpose of giving that incentive, and based on a program and on criteria which are well known. 1 put the question to the Minister again because we are talking about Estimates. Why did the Minister not come in today and show us in those Estimates of the Treasury Board that amount of money, that incentive which will be distributed to the managers?
I make that point seriously to the Minister. I fail to understand why that same amount of money, if it is available in a lump sum, cannot be given to the public servants on a merit principle. Why can it not be given to those who better perform, and not necessarily managers? The Minister knows I have gone through this over the years on the school boards. We tried to administer that kind of a program based on merit, better functioning and better efficiency, and that is difficult. I recognize it is difficult to have the criteria in place, but 1 want to know what our Government is going to do because it is important to me to know how the program is going to be put into effect.
I have spoken to managers and I am told by some that they do not want that money given to them on the basis of more efficiently cutting public servant jobs. The perception out there is that more money is given to managers if they cut programs or Public Service jobs. I do not believe the Minister is the type who would want to do that, but I do say to him that that is the perception out there. The average Canadian does not know what the Government means by an "incentive to productivity".
I plead with the Minister to come forward soon with the information concerning the sums of money involved. What are the criteria for access to these sums of money? What time span are we talking about? How will the program be administered?
I hope it will be a program based on merit and not on the efficiency of managers to cut programs. I hope that the method employed will not be the awarding of some type of bounty money to those who perform better in terms of their search for innocent people who are not for the Government's lack of direction.
I wanted to talk about the state of certain programs which the Government has put forward and which are included in the

Mr. Speaker, I would like to reply to the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) for whom I have the greatest respect. At the beginning of his speech, he talked about reductions affecting students or the student population. I would like to draw his attention to the fact that this new Government has prepared since it came into office, in 1984, 45 programs to assist students in Canada. We are not talking only of Vanier or Ottawa but of the whole country, including the Abitibi area, from east to west, as far as the Great North, and one could say that quite effective programs could be set up to help our students. There are exactly 45 programs. The record of this new Government is incredible. You should consult this blue guide on scholarships and grants offered by the Government of Canada that was prepared recently-a little publicity, in passing-which is a very good one.
You are saying that in the Ottawa area there is no construction activity, that building is not going well. However, when I come back from Abitibi, via highway 105, and I arrive in this area, I see construction everywhere. One Museum on one side, another one on the other, a Court House. Moreover, I recently stayed overnight in a hotel, the Westin, and I happened to talk with the owner who told me that during the summer his occupation rate was 92 per cent. I walked in the hotel and, in the lobby, I noticed that people were not from Ottawa, they were tourists. Some even came from as far away as China. There were also tourists from Vancouver. I then decided to call one of my good friends who runs a hotel on the other side, in Hull. The following day I asked him the same question: "Is the situation bad on your side"? He said: "No, my occupation rate improved this year and is about 70 per cent."
So, things are going pretty well now that we have a new Government. Promised, we won't talk about the past. It is mentioned almost every day in the House, but I respect you. We talk a lot about the Department of the Secretary of State ... We can see in the documents that there is an increase of $190 million for the Youth Employment Program which is
part of the Governement's strategy for jobs creation. A little further there is a $650 million increase for the Canadian Jobs Strategy announced in the Budget of May 1985. The increase in the number of man-years is offset by internal reallocation.
Looking at an other area, namely the Treasury Board, we have an increase of $17.4 million in employer contributions to insurance and pension plans due to higher rates. Then we see an increase of $2.4 million and thirteen person-years affected to the Privatization Secretariat responsible for following up on the decision to sell Crown Corporations.
When I come to this place to sit in the House or to work in my office for my constituency, I find that things are going well in Ottawa and even in the area around Ottawa. I tell the Hon Member that I find everything is going very well.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in the debate this evening, particularly to speak before my many Quebec colleagues, because I am very glad to belong to this Government. For two years now, Mr. Speaker, this Government has shown leadership as much in the field of employment as in the field of international relations.
Mr. Speaker, I am glad because I had the honour to belong successively to these two Departments. First I was Parliamentary Secretary for Employment and Immigration where I took an active part with the Hon. Flora MacDonald in the establishment of the new job-creation programs. Since last January, Mr. Speaker, I have been pleased to be associated with the Department of External Relations where, with the Hon. Monique Vezina, we are launching new programs and revised programs for foreign aid and assistance to Canadian companies.
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased as well to take part in this debate because I realize that our opponents have precious little to say because of our concrete results. Mr. Speaker, we have a positive record in both economic and financial sectors.
As you undoubtedly recall, the Minister said this on November 8, 1984: We must reduce the deficit. The way things were going, the deficit was to reach $39 billion. We will close the books next year with a deficit under $30 billion. We simply have to pay our debts.

speechtext:
They are the debts of the Liberals, but they are now our debts because we are now the Government. The House will recall that those people governed the country in the mid-seventies when the Minister of Finance mentioned earlier, Mr. MacEachen, announced a deficit of $19 billion. At the end of the year, we had a deficit of $31 billion or $32 billion. However, it was not serious! There was no problem because, at the time, the estimates were generous.
Some of my constituents asked me last week: What have you done for us, what has the Conservative Party done since the elections? It is very simple. We have establised a healthy economy in which the private sector will play a positive role to create jobs.
Mr. Speaker, when you can maintain some of the best interest rates-and they have now gone down-you have cause to rejoice. These are practical results which will not only encourage the Liberals to enter the House, but also give the private sector confidence in the Canadian economy.
This brings me to a specific point which concerns foreign aid. As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, at the very beginning of our mandate, we made a commitment to bring the amount of foreign aid up to a rather higher rate than we can actually achieve at this time. There has therefore been talk of major cut-backs. Contrary to what the Liberal speaker said earlier about education, I have to point out that you can speak either in terms of percentages or in terms of net amounts. In fact, we are going to allocate more money in net terms to foreign aid.
The Members opposite often accuse us of saying: Naturally, the Government helps other countries-and I can already hear the questions-when it is unable to help its own citizens. The Canadian public understands us. If we look at the survey on the famine in Ethiopia, we find that 95 per cent of Canadians agree with foreign aid. Indeed, when we help other countries, Mr. Speaker, we help Canadians to develop because we export not only our products, but also our talents. The names Canadian corporations are making for themselves in Africa and Asia are remarkable and recognized throughout the world.
Even if the growth is not as rapid as was foreseen in 1984, Mr. Speaker, we are going to reach just the same 0.5 per cent of our Gross National Product in terms of foreign aid in 198687. And this will have direct spin-offs for Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, this 0.5 per cent which will contribute to the integration of our private and public sectors to our foreign aid effort will be achieved following consultations and, finally, through cooperation.
I should like to deal first with consultations. People, Canadians or some of our friends could readily imagine that something like foreign aid is decided by some civil servant working behind the scenes, on the basis of current ideas and fashions, without too much planning.
Mr. Speaker, I had the privilege last January to take part in bilateral meetings with representatives from Niger, Senegal and Gabon, and more recently in Ottawa with those of

June 10, 1986
Supply
Burkina Faso and Zaire. Zaire was last week when we had the honour to welcome Mr. Mubutu Jr. who was here as Secretary of State to sign an agreement of co-operation and dialogue. Mr. Speaker, we spent these three days of negotiation planning our action on the African continent with the support of the Government concerned and in line with our major objective of food self-sufficiency. We had to touch on the problems of hydro power and desertification. Another point is the involvement of women in public affairs and affairs of the State. Tomorrow will mark the beginning of a very important program for the participation of women in development programs, for it is a well-known fact that in all countries which major development problems, and especially in Africa, women have a very significant role to play, and tomorrow will be an important day in that regard.
So after consultation, Mr. Speaker, we enter the concerted action stage because as we very well know Canada is not the only country involved in foreign aid. The World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, all those international institutions, the United Nations where again two weeks ago the Minister for External Relations (Mrs. Vezina) announced a 5-year moratorium on the African countries' indebtedness. As important as it may be, Mr. Speaker, to take any action as a country among foreign nations, such action must tie in with that of the large international institutions.
So this is stage two.
And stage three is cooperation, the most aggressive one for Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, we have agreements signed both with private industries and universities, labour unions, municipalities, provincial Governments, non-profit organizations that are helping us implement our international cooperation program.
We had recently the Minister for External Relations announce a $ 150-million program called Africa 2000 because it is aimed at Africa in the year 2000, and $150 million were ear marked for the next 5 years, and we agreed that 50 per cent of those funds will be managed by businesses, non-profit organizations. That is a major component of the new direction proposed by the Conservative Party for foreign aid. Governments have no monopoly as regards truth or positive moves in the area of development. This has already been seen in job creation programs. As we always said, jobs are not created by the Government. The Government will create economic conditions for jobs to be created, that is interest rates, investment programs to ensure that the economy by itself will take over.
It is time, Mr. Speaker, we stopped thinking that the federal Government or provincial Governments or for that matter municipal governments can do everything, that they have a monopoly on how to make things go.
Therefore, we will give the necessary tools to non-profit organizations, unions and universities the necessary tools and they will have to manage their business according to the
programs developped with the countries and co-ordinated with big international corporations.
In short, Mr. Speaker, such is the status of foreign aid programs and we know that they have been extremly successful. I only have to say in this House, Mr. Speaker, how proud I was to be with the Minister for External Relations in New York when she spoke. It was one of those special occasions in that lofty hall where a speech was interrupted by our warm applause.
It was quite important for Canada, and the critics were quite constructive about it, our country being a leader in international development, a movement followed by a few countries, perhaps not as much as we would have like, but this will be a landmark and following their return home after having seen the action of the Government of Canada, the other representatives could ponder over it. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I am proud to say the African and Asian countries as well as all the South American countries warmly applauded that initiative. I was pleased because a few weeks later, we had the honour of welcoming to Ottawa several of those African Ministers and others from other countries who were coming to meet us and tell us how pleased they were to see the constructive and stirring action of the Government of Canada.
This is in short, Mr. Speaker, how we are in a position to maintain our level of foreign aid in spite of reductions applied to all programs including international development. The following question was raised in the House: We are in favour of foreign aid, but reductions are required. Obviously, all Canadians understand the matter. We cannot ask Canadians to make sacrifices while we increase foreign aid. Our foreign and domestic programs will be subjected to the same reduction. However, we must maintain the same rate of growth, because if the Government is now experiencing temporary financial problems, we still have faith in the future. This is the reason why our aid programs are growing at a different rate which Canadians are in a position to sustain.
Well Mr. Speaker, that takes care of foreign aid. As for job creation, the figures speak for themselves and I need not delve into this because our record is going to be most positive. Some of my colleagues will certainly want to speak to it but in this area as in the other, we can see that Canadians are future oriented. We do have a certain tendency. As I was looking earlier at my colleague from Quebec East (Mr. Tremblay) tearing up his papers, it reminded me that there is a propensity to find scandals. My colleague from Quebec East is very aware of it; as a matter of fact, so I am told, they went through his wastebasket. That is why I believe he has good reasons to tear up his papers. They were trying to discover things the party might be doing wrong and that it could be blamed for. With that new approach, Mr. Speaker, if we take the time to look around, we can see that Canadian men and women agree with us and support the initiatives taken by the Government in foreign affairs as well as domestically.
June 10, 1986
