subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to enter the debate because it gives me a chance to bring to this House a question that needs to be dealt with, namely, the way we are handling our postal service.
I know that the postal service is not the highest matter on the political agenda. It is not often dealt with by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) or by the Leaders of the opposition Parties although it is a pretty important question to a lot of people. The postal service is vital to most average Canadians.
It is a service that people need and depend upon. It is a service that is not being delivered properly today, and it is a policy question that is being severely neglected by the Government.
The whole perspective from which the Government views the Post Office is a distorted one. It is coloured in ideological tones. When the Government speaks about the Post Office, it talks about deficits and eliminating the deficit in the Post Office. By choosing this language to speak of the Post Office, the Government is revealing its ideological bent and its distorted way of looking at an essential public service.
June 10, 1986

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext: The Government never talks about delivering the mail.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext:
The Government certainly does not talk about delivering the mail and the Government has not come up with any ways to meet that challenge. When the Government talks about the Post Office, it does not talk about a public subsidy or a public service. The Government does not acknowledge that other means of communication are subsidized.
For example, what about telephones? Just about everyone has a telephone in his or her home, although some people on low incomes do not, but telephone service is subsidized. In Manitoba we have a public telephone service, the Manitoba Telephone System. We can take revenues from the lucrative sections of the telephone market and use them to subsidize service for the average person. We can take profits from the revenues that we gain from long distance phone calls or from phone calls which large corporations make as a normal part of business activity and use them to subsidize service for the average citizen. Virtually everyone then can have a telephone and the rates can remain at a reasonable level. That kind of communication is subsidized. So why not subsidize the mail, which is another basic communication service? We subsidize air transportation. Surely no one is under the impression that air transportation is paid for simply by those who buy tickets when they choose to fly.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext: Especially the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext:
Or the Prime Minister with his private fleet of jets carrying along cameras to record "The Life of Brian". That service for a particular individual is subsidized. Surely most Canadians are aware that air travel is subsidized. I hope that the Government would not think of privatizing the airports in order that they not be subsidized publicly or not have a "deficit". The Government, of course, is very creative. I would not want it to take up that idea.
The trucking industry in the country is subsidized. That is another means of communication. The public pays for the roads. Obviously there are some taxes on the gasoline which trucking firms use, but the trucking industry is subsidized. There are all sorts of means of communications in the country which are subsidized. Therefore, why do we single out the Post office and say that there should be no subsidy for it? Why do we say that the Post Office is running at a deficit? Why is the Government so insensitive to the need for this basic service? Why does it not accept the fact that it is legitimate to subsidize a public service?
While the mails may seem like a dull, boring subject, it is something which touches all Canadians. For a mother writing to her son who is away from home attending university, a grandmother writing to her daughter who lives in another city, and a small business person carrying on normal business activities, this is an essential service. A good, sound postal
Supply
service is a means of economic development. It is part of the infrastructure which we need to have a good economy.
How many times have we heard that the vast majority of jobs today are created by small business? Large corporations are no longer the creators of employment. Who depends upon the mails? Is it the large corporate enterprise which can afford a courier service, or the small business person who needs that public service in order for his or her business to prosper?
I suggest that rather than considering the mails to be a drain on the public purse we should look upon it as an investment, as a part of the economic infrastructure which is necessary in order for small businesses to prosper and for communities to benefit from the employment creation capacity of small business.
When the Conservatives talk of deficits they talk from an ideological perspective. They talk from the perspective of government playing too large a role in society. They believe that in order to improve society we must downsize government and that if we do that we will all be more affluent. In fact, it has been suggested that one of the reasons the Government is starving the Post Office and moving in the direction of eliminating the public subsidy at the Post Office is that it wishes to privatize it at a later date.
Once the Government has weakened this service so badly and the public is fed up with the service, it will be publicly acceptable to sell it. Private firms can then cream off the most lucrative large urban markets for mail delivery. We will be left with a second class, bare bones service for other areas of the country which, of course, would have to be paid for out of the public purse. We would still end up having to subsidize this service.
In the last Budget the Government set the goal of financial self-sufficiency for the Post Office. When the Minister speaks of the Post Office in the House he talks about eliminating the deficit and improving service at the same time. We must be a little more realistic than to think that those two objectives can be met without a fundamental change of strategy by the Government.
We know that the Minister has been laying out new plans for the Post Office which he has failed to make public. He is examining options which he has not shared with the Opposition or the public. We believe that the reason he has not been open about his plans for postal service in the country is that his plans are bad news for the people. The plans are for continued and increased cuts in service. What other conclusion can we come to? If he had something to say which people might welcome, I assume he would be laying out his options so that we could all participate in debate and help him make the final decision. It looks very much as though he will be presenting a plan which will be bad news for the people. He is keeping it under wraps and will announce it at the last minute, perhaps on the last sitting day of Parliament or even after Parliament adjourns, hoping to escape public scrutiny and criticism.

June 10, 1986
Supply
If the Minister follows that sly route, if he continues to hide his plans for the Post Office and waits to announce them when the House is no longer sitting in order to avoid public criticism, he will not achieve his objective. If he announces these plans in the summer, the summer will not be quiet for him. We in this Party willl be here watching what he does. We will be waiting for his announcements. Whether he makes them while Parliament is sitting or in what he thinks will be the quiet of summer, we will be here to offer our analyses and critiques of his plans. It would be better for the Minister to share his thoughts about the Post Office with the public and to allow the public to assist him in making the decision.
To bring the issue of mail service closer to home, I point out that there are a lot of people in Canada today who are very angry about the lack of adequate postal service. I use as an example those people who live in new suburban developments. It has been brought to our attention that one developer in Ontario found it difficult to sell the houses he was building because of the lack of postal service. This actually had an impact on his ability to sell houses. People who are living in these communities are fed up and angry with the Government.
People in the community of Nepean, adjacent to Ottawa, mft,with the Minister responsible for the Post Office (Mr. Cote). He told them that he would not proceed with the installation of community post office boxes until after he had made decisions and his plans had been made public and that he would take their views into account. This very day the Post Office is dropping community boxes off in front of houses in the community of Fisher Glen in Nepean. The Minister said that would not happen until after a proper plan for the Post Office was put in place. The residents of that community were reassured when they first met with the Minister. They thought they would get some justice. They were, therefore, quiet about their anger with postal service. They were, therefore, quiet about the fact that they feel very strongly that they are being treated as second class citizens and being discriminated against.
They showed their anger about a week ago at a Nepean City Council meeting where the Post Office was presenting its plans. The city councillors, who are of course political leaders very close to people in their community, responded to that anger and passed a resolution asking their lawyers to take legal action against Canada Post. The resolution then went to the Federation of Canadian Municipalities, which represents communities like Nepean all across the country. The federation passed a resolution calling upon the Government to give fair and equitable service to all Canadians and to cease and desist discriminating against people living in new suburban developments.
The Government may think that postal service is a mundane matter which it can kind of leave on the sidelines and not pay much attention to. However, as I said before, all Canadians use the postal service so the vast majority are angry about
inadequate service and would like to see the Government take a real hand to develop a strategy which would result in fast, reliable delivery of mail.
People recognize that paying a reasonable subsidy to the Post Office for certain services is a legitimate activity for Government. What they are now beginning to realize is that this Government is more concerned about its own ideological commitment than it is about the feelings of ordinary Canadians. What I mean is that when the Government looks at the Post Office it sees a deficit. It then connects that with its overall plan to eliminate the national deficit, which will bring us to economic recovery and prosperity. However, we need to look at the Post Office on its own merits, not just from the perspective of subsidizing its deficit. We need to ask how we can devise a plan and objectives and priorities for the Post Office so that it will deliver adequate service. We have to recognize the need to subsidize public services. It is a legitimate activity for a Government and a legitimate use of public funds. In no way can it be equated with wasteful spending that Governments get involved in, such as this grandiose enterprise to film the Life of Brian. Perhaps the Government could save money on that kind of activity and devote some energy, thought and creativity to delivering a common, basic service to ordinary Canadians. They are demanding that service and they want it provided in an equitable manner.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the intervention from the Hon. Member. I appreciate the opportunity to respond directly to his points. I understand he comes from a rural riding, and I am sure he is aware that Canada Post is reducing
June 10, 1986

rural service and closing rural post offices. It has been doing so for some time now. It is also doing that without seeking the necessary Orders in Council. There is a provision under the Canada Post Corporation Act which says that if the Post Office is going to terminate a rural route or close a post office, it has to get an Order in Council before it does it. Canada Post is closing post offices and eliminating services in his riding, just as it is doing across the country, without getting Orders in Council. Why? Because if it gets an Order in Council there is a 60-day notice required and people are then able to express their views and appeal for redress.
The Government is turning a blind eye to the fact that Canada Post is ignoring its own Act and not giving people notice of a reduction in service. I am sure his constituents are as concerned as are other rural residents whom I have spoken to about adequate service and the way decisions about service are made.
The Hon. Member mentioned productivity of Post Office workers. The first principle of productivity is good management. You have to have well thought out objectives. You have to have a strategy to meet those objectives. The problem with productivity at the Post Office is that the Government has not thought through on how to deliver the service. The Government has not listened to Canadians to find out what their priorities are. It has not looked into how we can achieve those objectives and at the same time give workers a framework within which they can be productive. Without a strategy or plan you cannot have productivity. After all, you have to not only move fast but you need to have a direction in which to go.
If the Government is worried about having to subsidize the Post Office and does not want to do it any more, why does it not consider opening up lucrative areas of the private market for Canada Post to compete in, areas such as parcel delivery? That is a $1 billion market and Canada Post could gain a reasonable share and earn revenue which could then be used to cross-subsidize some basic services. I would like to suggest that one of the reasons the Conservative Government refuses to examine that as a policy option is that the Government does not want to get the business sector mad at it. It does not want the courier services to be angry at them. The Government prefers to have ordinary Canadians who want basic services angry, rather than to have a few large businesses angry at it. That shows the Government's ideological perspective and it shows who the Government listens to. What I am asking the Government to do is to listen to ordinary Canadians who are requesting just and expeditious mail service.

speechtext:
I wonder if the Member has noticed that over the last few years under the previous President of Canada Post there has been labour peace at the Post Office. The previous President, although we may have criticized him, and in many cases very legitimately, had a policy of communicating with people. He communicated with the public and he communicated with the unions. They did not always like to hear what he had to say, but he communicated. One thing that has happened since this Government appointed a new President of Canada Post is that there has been no communication. The doors have been closed at Canada Post. Canada Post does not communicate with the public, and neither does the Minister responsible for Canada Post. The Government is moving in ways that will antagonize and anger organized labour at the Post Office.
Just last Friday they dumped one of the labour representatives on the Board of Directors of Canada Post. They did not even talk to the Canadian Labour Congress who had the responsibility for appointing that person. The unions who work and represent the people at Canada Post have been trying, since the new President of Canada Post has been appointed, to have one meeting with him to talk about future prospects at Canada Post. This man refuses to meet with them, refuses absolutely. How do you expect to have a climate of cooperation and a climate that will ensure reliability of service if you do not communicate with people? One of the first lessons this Government has got to learn about the postal service is that if there is going to be good service and peace it has to start communicating.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak to the Estimates of the Department of Communications and Culture. I really should call this a reussite trompe-l'oeil. First, because it would seem as if the cultural sector has been reaping benefits over the past few months, but when one examines more closely the record of this Government, it is not quite so bright.
I suggest that we have been duped, and I would say it is the triptych art effect. It is a real trompe-l'oeil. The master has been at work creating the kinds of illusions that would make us feel that we have had a great buffet at the art and culture table.
Yes, activity and moneys have been allocated from the Department of Communications and Culture over the past few months. Let us look to see exactly what has happened. Let us examine the dramatic impact that the cultural sector has had upon the Canadian economy. Then let me focus on what has been happening in the various departments of this Ministry over the past year.
A number of task forces and papers have been initiated by the Minister; the task force on broadcasting at a cost of $2.8 million; the task force on national museums at a cost of $425,000; the task force on funding of the arts at a cost of $833 million; the task force on the film industry at a cost of $134,000; a task force on the National Arts Centre for $319,000; the Green Paper on cultural industries, and I do not have the cost for that; a white paper on the status of the artist at a cost of $50,000; and we have also had federal-provincial consultations for the development of a telecommunications policy. After all these task forces and these papers are collected, and after we, the taxpayers, have paid out in excess of $4,561 million, where are we?
The reports really need to be tabled and then, I guess, we should determine what kind of action to take, but certainly not precipitously, once having laid out taxpayers' money to this extent. Four million plus dollars is a lot of money. If we have
gone to this kind of trouble, why would we consider amending legislation prior to evaluating and examining and then taking these task forces' opinions and reports into serious consideration? Here we are contemplating legislative changes to the Broadcasting Act before we have even seen what the Caplan-Sauvageau report has to say.
Added to these expenditures, what about the millions of dollars spent by the Nielsen Task Force which, according to the arts and culture community, was ineffectively and inefficiently spent with very little consultative process? That is the Nielsen Report. All I can say is that we have had all the sectors of this particular part of our economy studied to death. We have had very efficient studies done prior to the arrival here of the new Government and there was action ready to be taken. With all those studies ready, we really did not need this delaying tactic of all the task forces. However, since they were put in place, let us at least consider them and take those opinions into account before moving ahead.
How was this illusion created? Why has the arts community drunk champagne and celebrated since that Budget night in February, 1986? The budget for the arts community was very good, and I think the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) should be lauded for his fine effort in dealing with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). In February, 1986, the Finance Minister announced the allocation of $75 million, beginning in 1986-87, to fund a number of cultural initiatives. These include $33 million to support the production and distribution of high quality Canadian feature films in domestic and world markets; $13 million to support a new book publishing development program which is much needed; $5 million in 1986-87 to assist the Canadian recording industry; $10 million to be allocated to the Canada Council in 1986-87 to increase its grants programs, including support for performing arts organizations; $3 million to compensate Canadian authors for the use of their works through public libraries; $7 million to allow the Public Archives to improve service; and $4 million to develop means of electronic sharing of information in the library data system. All of these grants have a problem associated with them, on which I will expand later.
I want to remind everyone that while they were busy drinking and eating at the feasting table, it was basically to drown some very sad memories. They will recall that this increase of $75 million does not make up for the cuts made in the November 1984 Economic Statement. Those cuts included the CBC cut-back of $75 million; the CBC high-tech cut of $10 million for equipment; $1.5 million from the National Film Board; $1.5 million from the CRTC; $1 million from the National Arts Centre; $3.5 million from the Canada Council; and budgetary cut-backs from different cultural projects and programs which amounted to $7 million. As well, the freeze on growth at 2 per cent caused a great loss over all. Increased radio licence fees and other charges amounted to $22 million. The grand total loss was $122 million. One only need do some
June 10, 1986

simple arithmetic to learn that the cultural and communication industries in Canada are left with a shortfall of $47 million, at a time when we know that everything costs more.
Let us consider the impact of cultural industries on our economy. I call to the attention of the House a quote by Henry Robertson Luce, who said: "The business of business is to take part in the great society."
Are we being allowed to take part in that great society to the extent that we can and should, particularly when we are being threatened with Americanization of our Canadian society?
Attempting to measure the contributions of culture to the economy must naturally rely on pragmatic definitions of culture. Unfortunately, this ignores all of the intangible and enabling characteristics which define us as a people. When we think of culture we often forget to include the economic contributions of culture. We must measure the economic impact of our cultural industries on our economy in terms of employment, wages paid, revenues generated and some of the other economic variables. Then we must compare this cultural aggregate with a similar total for the entire economy. Not surprisingly, the difficulty comes in deciding what to include in the list of cultural industries.
Statistics Canada includes eight categories when looking at the arts and cultural sector. They are the written media arts sector, which comprises the printing and publishing of books, newspapers and periodicals; the film industry; broadcasting, including radio, television, cable and pay-TV; the record industry, including the production and manufacture of recordings and the manufacture of musical instruments and artists' material; non-profit institutions, such as heritage institutions and libraries; the retail of cultural products such as books and records; the wholesale of cultural products; and Government involvement in the arts.
According to the analysis of Statistics Canada, the direct impact of the arts and culture sector as measured by the Gross Domestic Product-the value of production arising within the geographical boundaries of Canada-was valued at $5.2 billion or 1.7 per cent of the GDP of the whole economy in 1981. I will not deal with the communications sector tonight because it is a complicated area which involves figures that I would like to deal with at another time, in other circumstances.
However, let us address the financial question within the arts industry. The arts industry includes advertising, broadcasting, motion pictures, the performing and visual arts, publishing, and sound and video recording. Arts industry revenue increased 64 per cent, at an average annual rate of 13 per cent between 1977 and 1981, from $4.7 billion to $7.7 billion. I hope that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) does not look for more money from this sector. He should leave it alone because we need more. I want to point out that it was under a Liberal Government that we as Canadians flourished and grew in this vital sector of our economy.
A "census of manufacturers" comparison of the 20 largest Canadian manufacturing industries and the arts industry in
Supply
1981 reveals that the arts industry was the largest, with employment of 234,280; the sixth largest with salaries and wages of $2.5 billion; and the eleventh largest with revenue of $7.7 billion, equal to the Canadian telecommunications industry. As I have indicated, that is the other half of the communications sector with which the Minister deals.
Arts industry revenue amounted to 2.4 per cent of Gross National Expenditure. Using the Gross National Expenditure multiplier of 2.1, the income ripple effect of the Canadian arts industry was at least $16.3 billion in 1981, or approximately 5 per cent of Gross National Expenditure. I suggest that the Nielsen Task Force could have taken that into consideration.
The fine arts, in which the primary motivation is art for art's sake, also have a significant direct economic impact. While firm figures are not available, an estimate can be developed. In 1981-82, the Canada Council provided $39 million to some 793 arts organizations. On average, Canada Council support represented approximately 10 per cent of total expenditures by arts organizations, or $390 million. If one assumes that Canada Council supports about 85 per cent or 86 per cent of total fine arts activity, then the Canadian fine arts generated $449 million in direct economic activity in 1981. These are the latest figures that I have in this field.
If one assumes that earned revenue represented approximately 30 per cent of total expenditure, then it is estimated that spectators spent an additional $143 million on restaurants, bars, hotels, taxis and souvenirs, ancillary to ticket purchases. However, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) suggested that we close those facilities at the National Arts Centre and turn them over to the private sector.
Accordingly, in 1981, it is estimated that total fine arts-related expenditure was $592 million. Using the Gross National Expenditure multiplier of 2.1, the income multiplier effect of the fine arts was at least $1.2 billion.
There are two distinct arts-related employment populations. When we consider these jobs together, they include 414,000 workers, or 4 per cent of the Canadian labour force in 1981. In fact, arts-related employment is nearly as large as the agricultural labour force and total federal Government employment, including Crown corporations. The first group is the arts labour force which is made up of workers who use arts-related skills in their day-to-day jobs, such as artists and arts technicians, including curators, librarians and camera persons. Between 1971 and 1981, the arts labour force increased 74 per cent as compared to 39 per cent for the total labour force. In 1981, the arts labour force included 278,255 workers.
The second group is the arts industry labour force made up of workers employed in art industries such as advertising, publishing, motion pictures, live staged events, fine art schools, libraries, and so on. Only 35 per cent of the arts labour force are employed in the arts industry. Between 1971 and 1981, the arts industry labour force increased 58 per cent as compared to

39 per cent for the total labour force. In 1981, the arts industry labour force included 234,280 workers, of whom 52 per cent were men and 48 per cent were women, compared with 60 per cent men and 40 per cent women in the total labour force. Artists made up 24 per cent of the arts industry labour force, technicians 18 per cent, administrators 8 per cent and other support personnel, 50 per cent.
So much for the detail. Now let us look at the impact on a number of the concerned cultural industries or agencies. I would like to address my remarks with respect to the Canada Council, the National Arts Centre, the National Museum, the National Library and the Public Archives. Let us start with the budgetary restraints, which has been the situation for Canada Council. Between 1975-76 and 1984-85, inflation in Canada ran at an average annual rate of over 10 per cent. Prices more than doubled. While it seems that the war against inflation has been won, the real value of the parliamentary appropriation to the Canada Council decreased at an average rate of almost 1 per cent per year. During the same period, however, total federal current expenditures increased at an average annual rate of 2.6 per cent. In the February 1986 Budget, the Minister of Finance announced that an additional $10 million would be allocated to the Canada Council in 198687 to increase its grants, including support for performing arts organizations. There seems to be some controversy between the Canada Council and the Department of Communications over how this money will be administered. The Department is telling Canada Council that the money can only be used for support for the performing arts, while the announcement in the Budget indicated that the money was for all grant programs, including the performing arts.
The Department of Communications has said that if the money is not used for the performing arts then Canada Council will not receive the additional $10 million. So much for arm's length. I would suggest that that relationship between the Government and Canada Council is at risk. I might suggest that this arm's length is becoming more shoulder to wrist. And the situation still exists that Canada Council does not have its money.
Organizations in the arts community are telling us that they are worried about increasing interference from the government department itself, that once new programs are initiated and if they are jointly managed, new problems are going to be encountered.
Let us look at the National Arts Centre. Since 1978-79, there has been a widening gap between the actual annual appropriation from Parliament to the National Arts Centre and the appropriation if inflation were allowed for. At present, that cumulative gap is $17,338,000. Thus, the National Arts Centre has been expected since 1978-79 to conduct eight years of programming with less than seven years of funding. This has drastically reduced the centre's ability to dream the Canadian dream for the future. As well, there has been a lack of desire on the part of the Government to indicate funding to allow for long-range planning by the centre. This is considered
something of a handicap for an agency where commitments must be made often years in advance. As well, the National Arts Centre is restricted in its sources of funding. The tradition in Europe has been for the state to be the massive supporter of the arts, and the tradition in the United States has been to leave it to the private sector. Canada finds itself, as usual, half way between the two. Therefore, I would like to suggest that we have to find Canadian solutions to Canadian problems.
I would like to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, the thoughts of Don MacSween, Director General of the National Arts Centre, who said:
-We begin a dream-but this is a dream, as they say, like a play. It is a play in progress. And it is so short a distance, financially, between fulfilling that dream and letting it die.
It is a short distance. I would like to suggest that we do not sacrifice our culture and creative juices. Yes, I know it takes money and that we have to tighten our belts right now. But if the Minister of Finance can find $1 billion to save the depositors who already received $60,000 as a result of the Western Bank disaster, $600 million to assist in the purchase of Gulf Canada and some $56 million to change the colour of our soldiers' uniforms, I would hope he could find the needed funds for the balance of our agencies. At some other time I will deal with the National Museums, the Archives and the National Library.
I would say that the buffet table to which we went is short of a considerable amount of dollars. We have not found all the answers to funding. I would like to recommend strongly that since the cultural community needs more dollars, we should move as quickly as possible, following the tabling of the Caplan-Sauvageau Report, the Museum report and other reports, so that we can rectify this problem within this constituency.

As the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) said this morning, he was delighted to announce that for the second consecutive year, the rate of growth of our expenditures was virtually zero. And if we take into account the $500 million cutback, the rate of growth is 0.2 per cent, like last year.
We have to go back to the immediate post-Korean War period, as the Hon. Member for Chambly (Mr. Grise) said, to find such a low rate of growth in the Government's operating expenditures for two years in a row.
Mr. Speaker, this very modest growth rate stands in sharp contrast to what this country has seen in the past under the Liberal Government. For fourteen years, from 1979 to 1984, the average annual growth rate in the voted portion of the Main Estimates ... you voted yourself during that time, and I am referring to the Hon. Member for Bourassa (Mr. Rossi)... the average annual growth rate reached a high of 36.8 per cent in 1975-76. It was not coincidence that such a situation prompted the Auditor General, Kenneth Dye, to declare in his report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1976, that Parliament and indeed the Government had lost or were about to lose effective control of the public purse, and that was our emphasis during the last election campaign. The previous Government had lost control over public expenditures, so the
people gave us their confidence and I am sure they are not disappointed this evening.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians put their faith in this Government because they realized that we were qualified to improve management here. We were faced with an undescribable administrative chaos.

So we restored order and used common sense in financial matters. It is unfortunate that the media do not comment on this very often, but knowing that millions of Canadians are watching Commons proceedings on television this evening, they will be able to find out what we have accomplished.
Over the last 20 months, Mr. Speaker, a number of measures have been implemented to restore efficiency in the management of personnel, programs, and assets of the federal public sector, something which we had not seen for quite some time. The impact of these measures can now be seen not only in our efforts to ensure a strong economic recovery, but also in the Government's commitment to give top priority to productive public affairs management.
We draw some inspiration from the private sector in Canada and, since I come from a region which has been described as the kingdom of small-and medium-size businesses, I am in a position to tell you that our Government has made the right decision. The most obvious indication of its management initiatives is the substantial reduction in expenditures and the increase in revenues which were achieved in response to our commitment to lower the deficit and to manage more efficiently the federal programs and organizations which are our responsibility. In a broader context, Mr. Speaker, the various management improvement measures taken by the Government during the last year and a half will have wide-ranging consequences on the future management of Government human and financial resources, as well as on the allotment of resources to federal programs and organizations. The total effect of these measures will be to create a framework in which Public Service managers will have the means and the incentive to manage public funds economically, efficiently and effectively.
First, in terms of significant measures, let us look at human resources management and the implementation of a comprehensive framework for human resources planning which incorporates management of this vital resource with program and expenditure planning and management. We have also suggested an improvement in labour-management relations including a comprehensive approach to contract negotiation, reinforcement of the staff relocation policy and agreements on principle about a major reform of Public Service pension plans and the development of a dental insurance plan, a voluntary early retirement program for senior public servants and managers to give new career opportunities to talented Public Service managers, the launching of a joint union-management
June 10, 1986

initiative on the principle of equal pay for work of equal value to develop an action plan to apply this basic principle throughout the Public Service, as well as the resumption of collective bargaining after expiry of the six and five wage restriction program and the successful negotiation of moderate pay increases in accordance with the difficult financial position of the Government.
It has also been proposed that we re-instate performance incentives for Public Service administrators by applying the principle of remuneration based on merit which had been fully applied only in two of the eleven previous years and that we implement a new productivity premium system to put even more emphasis on efficient and economical management in the Federal Public Service.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank you for your wise decision. I think if I started counting all the friends of the Liberal Party who benefitted under this plan for 25 years, it would take me all night.
Another example of good manaqgement, Mr. Speaker. In 20 months, the Conservatives have reduced the number of Government flights by 22 per cent and the number of flying hours by 23 per cent, as compared with a 12-month period under the Liberal Government, resulting in savings of $2.5 million. That is how we see it.
Mr. Speaker, in the May Budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced cutback objectives totalling 15,000 person-years in those parts of the Public Service under the jurisdiction of Treasury Board.
These reductions, spread over five years, will start in fiscal year 1986-87, with a 2 per cent reduction from the 258,222 person-years indicated in the Main Estimates for 1985-86. These cutbacks will continue at the rate of 1 per cent annually, until 1990-91.
Mr. Speaker, in 1986-87 these cutbacks will save $150 million, which will be applied to reduce the deficit, and when the cutback objective of 15,000 person-years is reached in 1990, the accumulated savings will exceed $1.5 billion, while recurring annual savings will be about $0.5 billion.
The Government intends to reduce the size and cost of the permanent Public Service required to administer federal programs, while at the same time ensuring that essential aspects of Government such as service to the public, transportation and security services are maintained. This is very important.
The reductions will be achieved thanks to increased productivity, the privatization of certain federal activities and, should it turn out to be profitable, the signing of deals for certain others.
The measures advocated by the Task Force on Program Review will continue to enable the Government to single out those sectors where person-year reductions might be needed because of duplication or program redundancy.
In this context, every effort has been made and will continue to be made to achieve cut-backs through attrition. Innovative staff redeployment policies which were endorsed by public service unions before implementation in 1985 will contribute to reduce lay-offs to a minimum.
Mr. Speaker, the Treasury Board policy will continue to be that any approved inclusion of person-years in Supplementary Estimates during a given fiscal year that deviates from cutback objectives, be compensated during the same fiscal year by cancelling person-years authorized in other controlled parts of the Public Service.
The President of the Treasury Board was very pleased this morning to talk about his new initiatives which will have a positive influence on the whole Public service and on Government spending.
The Treasury has administered our finances wisely. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that we should be confident that this Government, in the second half of his mandate, will restore order to the Public service and breathe some fresh air into programmes which, in many cases, were contrary to public interest.
Now that the deficit is reduced and under control, I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians will appreciate what we have done to lower the very heavy deficit we inherited when we took over.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that it would be very much in order that we congratulate tonight the President of the Treasury Board and his staff.

Mr. Speaker, in the few moments left in this debate there are one or two things that I want to say. I have been somewhat perplexed over the course of almost two years by the Government's reliance on polling to tell the Government what it should or should not be doing. Hidden in the expenditure Estimates that we are about to approve this evening are countless numbers of dollars that have been used by the Government to poll the public of Canada in an attempt to satisfy on a day-to-day basis what certain people might believe is necessary.
First, about polling, it is interesting that this Government like the last Government has found its own polling companies among its friends spending tens of thousands, if not millions, of dollars on pollsters, supplying them with a steady stream of money day after day, week after week, year after year to try to identify what it is the public of Canada really wants. Why is the Government doing this? The Tory Government is doing this because, when it started out, it did not have any policy worth talking about.
I think we can all remember the Tories saying that they were going to be a better Government, whatever that means. They were going to be better than the Liberal Government. That is certainly rising to great heights. However, the Tories were going to be better than the previous Liberal Government. Better at what, Mr. Speaker? The Tories said they were going to be better at a number of things but they did not tell us they were going to be better at patronage. They are better at that. They did not tell us they were going to be better at spending money on their friends in order to keep them in business, but they are better at that.
I thought tonight I would take a moment or two to run over some of the things that people I know are concerned about. Earlier this evening I took a few moments and did a poll of my own. I thought to myself that it might be helpful to seek out from some average, albeit some young, Canadians what they thought they would like to hear the Parliament of Canada speaking about. What is it they are concerned about that they do not hear addressed on a regular basis? What is it that these young people would like to have heard spoken about tonight but until now they have not been able to hear about? Let me run through quickly what they said because I think it is enlightening to say the least. It does reflect a concern not only of those individuals, but I suspect-in fact I am sure-a concern of a large number of people in that age group, in the late teens and early twenties, who live in many parts of Canada and who represent, if one were to test it accurately, a good cross-section of the population of Canada in that age group. What did they say to me? They asked, why is Parliament not talking about the cost of university funding? Why is there no emphasis placed on the cost to young people of
June 10, 1986

providing themselves with an education in order that the future of Canada could be secured?
I wondered about that. I realized that the next point raised was tied in very closely to it. The next young person to whom I spoke said: "I do not hear much being said about jobs for youth". You can see the tie-in right away. Young people wanting not only to improve themselves but to improve the society in which they live cannot get the money from the sources that used to make money available. Neither can they find jobs, jobs that they need in order to survive not only for the purpose of going to school but for the purpose of developing skills and of providing for the future.
I then asked what other area they thought the Parliament of Canada ought to be discussing on this important evening as we set about to vote on an expenditure of $116 billion plus. I said that maybe Parliament should discuss the Government's propensity to subsidize business. Why is it that the Government seems to be able to find money to subsidize business through various tax relief programs, directly through government grants, and through all kinds of agreements it enters into through services rendered or not rendered depending upon who you listen to, but cannot find money to put into jobs for youth and cannot find money to provide young people with an opportunity to complete their education?
As we pursued the matter I asked whether there were any other questions which they felt the Parliament of Canada ought to be dealing with. You, Mr. Speaker, will not be surprised to hear this, and I know that the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) will be in full support of it. Within the Bill which we will be dealing with in less than 20 minutes there is little, if anything, to encourage anyone in Canada to believe that the Government is committed in any way, shape, or form to pursuing the goal that the majority of young Canadians believe is important, that being nuclear disarmament.

We did not win, but many of those who have been in the finals in years gone by did not win this year either. Not to have succeeded this year in getting into the final round is hardly a measure of Canada's ability to participate.
Young people told me that if we are going to do better, if we are going to raise Canada's image in the world, if we are going to have quick and valuable recognition of the worth of the youth of Canada, the Parliament of Canada should take some time to talk about activities in sports and physical fitnesss.

The Parliament of Canada should set aside just a little bit of time to discuss that aspect of cultural and physical life in Canada. From that we draw world recognition and significant benefit. One cannot find much to commend that in these particular expenditures.
I was asked where the expenditure is on cultural and foreign exchange. How do we get to know about what goes on in other parts of the world? Where is Canada's commitment to educating our young people about the nature of life in the rest of the world? How do we encourage young people from other parts of the world to come to Canada to find out about the kind of democratic society in which we live, the kind of opportunities which exist here, and the way in which we have developed? Where do we find within these expenditures the necessary dollars for that kind of undertaking? They are not there.
If we are going to play a role in the world-and there are many who think we can, including myself-if we are going to be a leader within the Commonwealth and if we are going to have something to say about what is going on in South Africa, Central America and other parts of the world which are facing tremendous economic and social upheavals, we must understand on a first-hand basis the activity and lifestyle within those countries.
Where do we find the necessary moneys to ensure that our youth are able to learn about those kinds of problems which are absolutely foreign to the lifestyle of most Canadians? How do we get young people to understand what it is like to go to bed at night and not know whether you will wake up in the morning? How do you get them to understand the kinds of atrocities which are being committed in South Africa without showing them, either directly or by clear indication, what is going on in those parts of the world? How do we encourage people there to continue their struggle for a democratic society if, when we look at the expenditures of one of the Governments in a free part of the world which has the capacity to generate wealth, we see no clear expenditure to enable our youth to

become educated in those very important human world-type problems?
I, therefore, suggest that the little poll I took is much more reflective of what the public of Canada is thinking about than is the poll taken by Gallup, the poll taken by Angus Reed, or the polls taken by any number of other pollsters. The poll that is important is the poll you take by speaking to people in Canada and asking them what debate they would like to take part in if they could be in Parliament tonight. The things I am mentioning are the things which the youth of Canada are now concerned about.
There are those in Canada who continue to be concerned, with justification during this Government's regime, about ensuring that we recognize, not only the duality of our country but also its multicultural nature. We must recognize the necessity to draw into the Canadian process, the parliamentary process, a good cross-section of those who represent a variety of cultures.
How do we tell people that we are doing our best in that regard when, as my colleague from Thunder Bay constantly says, we cannot even work out a satisfactory arrangement with the Japanese Canadians who were denied their human and civil rights during the Second World War? How do we hold ourselves up as champions of a multicultural society? Where do we find in these expenditures moneys sufficient to meet our obligations to those people? My colleague has constantly raised this with the Minister who is now responsible for the issue and with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and others.
What response do we get? The Government says that it would like to do something as long as it does not cost very much. It would like to recognize the problem, but it would not like to recognize it financially. The Government hopes that somehow or other it will be able to get the problem resolved, but it certainly would not want it to be resolved if it will cost the coffers of Canada a great deal of money. I happen to believe, as many of us do, that the time has come to sit down and negotiate fairly. That is reflected in the attitude of the young people I spoke with here this evening.
Having gone over the expenditures of Government, having spoken to people who will be the parliamentarians of the future, people who represent the dream of Canada, I know they do not believe for one minute that the topics being discussed here tonight speak to this country's future. They do not believe for one minute that contained within the expenditure program of this Government are the necessary funds, properly allocated, to guarantee that those kinds of pursuits will become a reality, that there is a clear indication by the Government that it wants to see change in those areas.
What we have seen over the last two years is a disaster. It is a shame. We have seen this Government elected on a big lie. It has now undertaken to attack the people of Canada. It is attacking everyone at every level. It started out attacking
pensioners. Had it not been for my colleague from Beaches, among others, and the efforts of the pensioners themselves all across this land, the Government would have totally eliminated indexation of old age pensions.

speechtext: Immediately. During the debate we even had a dispute between the Ministers involved, the Prime Minister on the one hand and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on the other, as to what they really intended to do. However, no amount of obfuscation on their part could in any way hide the truth from our pensioners. They knew. They could see it. They were out on Parliament Hill fighting against this Government in order to maintain what they had fought for for years.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext: The Government cut back on EPF funding, and what did that mean? It meant less money for universities, higher tuition fees, fewer opportunities, a reduction in Canada's productive capacity, and it means that Canada will not keep pace with technology. What does the Government do? It attacks the youth as it attacks the pensioners. Then we come to the workers of Canada. Where was the Government when Ronald Reagan decided to slap on all kinds of tariffs? Where was it when he moved to cut back on the imports of Canadian softwood lumber? Where was it when the U.S. moved to cut back on hogs and fish imports? Where was it when the U.S. brought in a Farm Bill which will undercut, in many ways destroy, markets which have long been held by Canada to be ours? Where were the Tory Members? You do not hear from them. They never speak for the people. They do not even understand the problem.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext: They are anonymous.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext: Then we have the former leadership candidate for the Tory Party, Peter Pocklington. Enough said. I do not have to go into any detail about that. We all well understand where the Tories get their policy from when you look at this man who ran for the Tory leadership and then takes the kind of action he is now taking.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext: Now we all understand why you are quitting.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext: Is it not bad enough to attack the pensioners and the youth? Is it not bad enough that they fail to support the workers of Canada? No, they then go on to change the unemployment insurance system. They go out and encourage people to take early retirement. Retire early, make room for young people, take lower paying, part-time jobs. Get out of the workforce.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext: Is that why you are leaving?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext:

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext: Is that reasonable? Is that the way one would expect a Government to operate? This Government has launched an attack on the people of Canada, but who has it helped?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext: The ordinary Canadian.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext:
You know whom they helped. The moment the banks got in trouble, remember that? When farmers were losing their farms because they could not pay their mortgages, when families were losing their homes because they could not meet their commitments, where was the Government? Day after day we said, give them some help. Oh, no. The Government said that this is a problem for the banks. When the banks were losing money, where did they get it from? Out of the pockets of the farmers who lost their farms and the families who lost their homes.
You will not be surprised, Mr. Speaker, to hear my final word is this. We will not support this Government's expenditure program.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1987
speechtext: Hear, hear!
